speechtext: I call the attention of the government to the statement of the right lion, the Prime Minister, on the lltli of March, with reference to certain papers respecting the claim of Mackenzie & Mann. On that date, in answer to a question, the right hon. gentleman said : That a certain claim had been made, and was being considered by the government, and that the papers would shortly be communicated to the House. Inasmuch as some four weeks have since elapsed, and the papers have not been brought down, I take the liberty of bringing the matter to the attention of the right hon. gentleman.

The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (Hon. Sydney Fisher) moved third reading of Bill (No. 32) to provide for the marking and inspection of packages containing fruit for sale. He said : When this Bill was discussed in the committee the other night, there was a considerable number of alterations made in various sections which will necessitate further alterations to make the Bill intelligent and complete. The proposed changes do not interfere with the principle of the Bill. The Bill as introduced was only intended to apply to apples and pears, but as it has been made to apply to all fruit, we shall have to substitute the word ' fruit ' for the words ' apples and pears,' in the sixth and seventh sections. In consequence of the introduction of clause 9, the words which deal with the size of the fruit are not required. In section 8, the word ' first ' should read ' finest.' In clause 9, line 20, the words ' The marks on such packages or' are not required. I withdraw my motion for third reading.
Motion for third reading withdrawn.
That the order for third reading of Bill (No. 32) be discharged, and that' the Bill be referred back to Committee of the Whole.

Motion agreed to, and House again went into committee on the Bill.
On section 6,
I move that the word 'fruit' be substituted for the words 'apples or pears,' and that all the words after ' package ' in the eighth line be struck out.
Is this intended to apply to tomatoes ?	"
I do not think tomatoes would come under the definition of fruit, but I would not like to give a legal opinion upon it.

Would you give us an agricultural opinion upon it ? I think Mr. HAGGART.
the hon. minister ought to be able to determine whether a tomato is a fruit or a vegetable.
I am not going to enter upon any such question.
I think what the hon. gentleman should decide first is what he means by fruit, because there is no definition in the Bill.

I would move that section 7 be amended by the substitution of the word ' fruit ' for the words ' apples or pears ' in the second line, and by striking out all the words after the word ' packed ' in the seventh line.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Perhaps the minister will insert a clause defining what fruit is to mean, because the word covers a large field. He would not say to my hon. friend whether a tomato is fruit or a vegetable.

I confess that I have not undertaken to define the word ' fruit ' in this Bill. I think the practice in the market would pretty thoroughly define it. The differences between a tomato and say a currant and a gooseberry are a little indefinite, if you say that the one is a fruit and the other is not a fruit in a scientific sense, although I think there is no doubt that in the courts a gooseberry would be considered in the market acceptation of the term a fruit, while in most cases a tomato would be called a vegetable. I do not think there is any very clear line of demarcation between a fruit and a vegetable.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Where would my hon. friend place a cranberry ?

I think the market definition of a cranberry would be that it is a fruit. To state arbitrarily that certain things are fruits and certain other things are not fruits would load down the Bill with complications ; and in making out such a list, something might be omitted which should not be omitted.

I think the minister's explanation is the strongest reason why there should be a defining clause. He suggests that it should be left to the courts to determine. It seems to me there is no necessity for that. Why not mention apples, pears, and certain other fruits in the Bill, and then anything outside of those would not be a fruit ?

To avoid all trouble it seems to me that you should not attempt to define fruit at all. For instance, would you call a banana a fruit ? It seems to me that what is understood in the commercial world as fruit is sufficient. As a rule, tomatoes are not put up in packages, so that this Bill does not apply to them.
I submit that the easiest way out of the difficulty would be to enumerate what fruits you are legislating about. Then you do not have to say what things are fruits and what things are not.

At least the hon. Minister of Agriculture might let us know what fruits he has in mind to which this Bill shall apply. When he is making a change from apples and pears to fruit in general, he must have in his mind certain fruits to which the Bill is to apply ; and it would perhaps give us a better idea whether the amendments are proper ones to be made, if he would state what those fruits are.

I may say to my hon. friend that the amendment does not propose to change the Bill beyond what was accepted in the committee. The provisions relating to apples and pears were originally intended to apply only to the export trade ; but when it was decided that they should apply to internal trade as well as to the export trade, there was no reason why they should not apply to all fruits, as the other sections do. That is the reason why I was obliged to make this change in the wording of this particular section ; and it is only a change of the wording. I must say that I think it would be difficult to make out a list of fruits to which only this Bill should apply. It might be done ; but there would be great danger that some fruits which are sold in the ordinary market might be omitted through inadvertence. I do not think there is any doubt in any ease which might arise under the Bill, the courts would be able to decide whether a particular fruit came under this Act or not.

I do not think the reason the hon. minister gives us is a sufficient reason to justify us in not amending the Bill at this stage. Even if this defect in the Bill has only now been brought to our attention, it is none the less the part of wisdom to insert a provision to overcome that defect. The minister says that if we Inserted a schedule of the fruits to which this Bill should apply, it might be found afterwards that other fruits should have been included. If so, it is an easy matter afterwards to amend the Bill so as to include them. But I think it is the part of wisdom to insert some list, so that the people handling, packing or selling fruit will know to what the Bill does apply.

It seems to me that the amendment which the hon. minister proposes is a little more important than he seems to imagine. The Bill originally applied, of course, only to apples and pears. These sections which the hon. gentleman is proposing to amend he proposes to make applicable to every variety of fruit. Therefore, as affecting all varieties of fruit except
apples and pears this has all the effect and importance of a new Bill. It does not seem to me worth while, then, to speak of this as a mere verbal change, a change of no importance. I do not know what other fruits besides apples and pears are usually sold in closed packages in Canada. The hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Fisher), having experience in his department with regard to such matters, should be able to inform the House on that subject. I would much like if the hon. gentleman would do so before the discussion goes further. It seems to me we are entitled to have that information from the hon. minister.
I understand that the change in these words affects other classes of fruit, but the change made proposes simply to carry out what I understood to be the intention of the committee.
With respect to apples and pears ?

With respect to all fruit. I supposed that these amendments had been made in committee, and it was only when I saw the reprinted Bill and found that these amendments had not been introduced that I proposed this change. As I understood the sense of the committee when the Bill was under discussion before, it was fully understood and intended that these sections should apply to all fruits. That is why I said that this was only a verbal alteration, and not because I did not understand or appreciate that the amendment made a radical change in the application of these two sections. As to the kinds of fruit that are sold in closed packages, peaches are frequently so sold and sometimes also currants, gooseberries and raspberries. Grapes are sold in closed packages, though the wording of the Bill applies only to kegs, barrels, or boxes, and would not apply to baskets. That change was accepted in deference to the representations of the hon. member for South Wentworth (Mr. Smith). When I said that it would be a difficult matter to make a list of fruits packed in closed packages, it was because there may be fruits which to-day are not sold in closed packages but which to-morrow might be so sold, in which case the Bill would apply to them. The Bill applies to every kind of fruit sold in a package which is of such a character as to prevent the buyer seeing and judging of the quality of what he is getting. The object is to assure the buyer of really getting what the seller pretends to sell. That being the general character of the Bill, it seems to me that the question of the kind of fruit is only a detail. The Bill applies to all fruits which are sold in such a way that the package may help the palming off on the purchaser of fruit of a lower quality than that represented by the seller. Fruits that are sold in open packages for home consumption are

frequently packed in closed packages for export. For instance, grapes are sold In open baskets in the local market, but they are sometimes exported in kegs, packed In various kinds of packing, such as buckwheat hulls and other things that are tasteless. This Bill would apply to grapes so packed. These are the reasons why, at the moment it strikes me as being inexpedient to define too closely the exact kinds of fruit to which the Bill should apply.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
I would like to ask the hon. minister how the Bill would apply to what we know in Ontario as the huckleberry, or the blueberry, as it is called in the lower provinces. We import this fruit largely from the lower provinces, and it comes packed in an enclosed package-a log hollowed out something like a sap trough and covered with a solid board. Those that come from the west are usually packed in pails. How would section 7 apply to the huckleberry if it were made to read

No person shall sell, or offer, expose or have in his possession for sale, any fruit packed in a olosed package, upon which package Is marked the grade ' No. 1 Canadian ' unless such fruit consists of specimens of one variety, sound, of fairly uniform size, and not less than SO per *cent free from scab, worm holes, bruises and other defects-
-and so on. When we get these berries from Nova Scotia, there is not twenty per cent of them but are bruised. Of course everybody will admit that the blueberry is a fruit, and it cannot be doubted that as we import them they are contained in a closed package. How will this Bill affect the trade in this fruit ?

If the mark indicated in the section is put upon the package, it will come under the operation of the section. If not, it will not come under the operation of the law. The seller is able to sell the fruit without putting on the packages the mark ' No. 1 Canadian? and without that it would not come under the section.

All this seems to make it more evident that it is important to define the kind of fruit aimed at by this section 7. Does the hon. minister pretend that those who gather blueberries, say, in the Saguenay district of the province of Quebec, are to be brought under the operation of this section ? How can they avoid violating the law
By not putting the mark upon them.

But they are obliged to put a mark on them. Under section 4, every person who packs fruit in a closed package for sale must mark the package

-(a) with the initials of the Christian names, and the full surname and address of the packer (b) with the name of the variety or varieties ; and
(c) with a designation of the grade of the fruit.
And how about the other wild berries picked in Quebec and sent to Montreal in closed packages ? How about the wild grapes that are sent to Montreal in barrels or closed packages in the autumn in very large quantities and are used in the city for different purposes ? How about the fruit known as mCire, or catlierinette ? Is my hon. friend going to apply section 7 to them ? It would be a frightful hardship on those who gather these wild fruits.

If a mark is put upon a closed package, indicating that it contains a certain quality of fruit, it ought to contain that quality of fruit. Of course, if one is attempting to sell in closed packages fruit which is not up to the quality represented on the packages, he would be guilty of an infraction of the law. And that is the intention.

Would the hon. minister explain the difference between ' grade ' and ' quality.' If they do not mean the same thing, they mean substantially the same, or they are so intimately connected that It would be difficult to distinguish between them.
I do not think there is any distinction.
Then my hon. friend (Mr. Monk) is right in saying that with this change all fruit in closed packages must be marked with the designation of the quality and so on.
Yes.
Then there would be no escape such as the hon. minister has pointed out.

But the object of the Bill is to prevent persons putting upon closed packages marks indicating that the fruit is of first quality when, as a matter of fact, it is not of first quality. If it is not the intention that the Bill should carry out that idea, these sections are not right.

Section 8 brings these two together, because it says :
No person shall sell, or offer, expose or have in his possession for sale any fruit packed in closed package, upon which package is marked any designation which represents such fruit as of first, best or extra good quality, unless such fruit consist of well-grown specimens of one variety, sound, of nearly uniform size, of good colour for the variety, of normal shape, and not less than 90 per cent free from scab, worm holes, bruises and other defects, and properly packed.
That leaves no possible escape. If there is anything that designates the quality of the fruit, and if the fruit is in an inclosed package, it comes within the operation of the law.
That is the intention of the Act.
It seems to me it may be a very serious matter.

As to the operation of the Act, it is very desirable that some such Act should be passed. My hon. friend must not think that we are opposed to the principle of the Act, because we are not; but it is necessary for us to see how it will work out. Take the case which was suggested a moment ago by my hon. friend from Leeds (Mr. Taylor), the bringing of blueberries from the maritime provinces to Ontario in closed packages. They might be in such a condition when they started upon their journey as to justify the application of grade No. 1, or A No. 1 ; and yet when they arrived at their destination they might be bruised, as he mentions. The result of that would seem to be that you would have to open every package and turn out a -sample of the fruit before you can sell it, otherwise the vendor would subject himself to a penalty under the interpretation of this Act which the hon. gentleman insisted on the other day. Now that does seem to be a result we would hardly like to bring about, and I would like to have the hon. gentleman's views with regard to it.

Before the minister makes his explanation, I would like to ask if all the fruit within the meaning of that section is supposed to be absolutely free from every possible defect ? If so, it is a very harsh Bill. The hon. gentleman will see that the Bill originally intended to indicate the defects that particularly belong to apples and pears, namely, scab, worm holes and bruises. But there are other defects. I would like to ask the minister if it is the intention that every class of fruit under section 6 must have 90 per cent absolutely free from every defect ?
The intention of the section as now amended would be that any fruit marked A No. 1 Canadian should be like that.

Does the hon. gentleman intend that all fruit marked A No. 1 Canadian shall stand first, and the fruit coming under section 8 shall stand second, and the fruit coming under No. 1 Canadian in section 7, stand third ? Because that would be the effect of the Bill by reason of 90 per cent being required under section 6 and under section 8, while only 80 per cent is required under section 7.

No, No. 8 is a different section altogether from sections 6 and 7. No. 8 is practically the same as No. 6 except that it does not give an absolute grade of a certain character, or brand of a certain character ; but it does not define the brand ; whereas No. 8 does give a definite brand of A No. 1 Canadian. But there is no comparison, or gradation, or inferiority of the fruit as sold under the definition in section 8, from that under section 6. I may say in reply to the hon. leader of the opposition, that section 6 as applied to a fruit like blueberries, or as applied to certain other small fruits, does not seem to be very clear. I think the description of the defects in them would hardly apply to such small fruit. It seems to me if it is only applied to apples and pears, a number of other fruits which would come legitimately under this section would escape and the section would not apply to them. But section 8 is really the section that would cover most cases. Sections 0 and 7 are those under which only certain specified grades are employed, and anybody selling such fruits as blueberries and other small fruits would not use these particular definitions of A No. 1 Canadian, or No. 1 Canadian, and consequently sections 6 and 7 would not apply to them ; while section 8 would apply to them if sold under any qualification, that is to say, if they put any brand upon them which indicated superior excellence. If they did not put a brand on them which indicated superior excellence, then section 9 would apply to them, and it requires that when the fruit is examined, the portion examined shall be a fair representative of the contents of the whole package.

I think section 7 will give rise in the province of Quebec to a great deal of useless litigation, because the definition therein is not correct at all as applied to fruit in general. The minister may say that when it is a question of small fruit, you won't turn to sections 6 or 7, but you must. There was a prohibition in section 7 which was limited to apples and pears, and it is now desired to apply it to all fruits, that is a prohibition to sell.
No, there is only a prohibition to sell with a certain mark upon them.
But does the minister suppose that parties who send blueberries and wild grapes fresh to Montreal will neglect to mark them as No. 1, because they must mark them.
Unless they mark them No. 1 Canadian this section would not apply.

In the first place, you say that all fruit must be marked with the designation or grade, it does not matter whether it is first, second, or extra quality or any quality. That, I take it, applies to all the fruit that is included in this Bill. Therefore you cannot exempt any kind of fruit from sections 6, or 7, or 8. I understood the minister to say that unless it is marked best, or extra good quality, it would not come under section 8 ; but they have got to mark the quality.
But they need not mark it extra good.
But there is either, first, best, or extra quality, these are the three qualities. But section 4 says you must mark the package with the grade of the fruit.
Yes, but if your fruit is not of extra good quality you can mark it medium, or mark it second, or whatever you like. You must mark the grade, but you may mark it second grade.
But suppose you do not mark them at all ?
But you must.
Then you are amenable to the law and liable to a fine if you do not mark them ?
No doubt.
Then if you mark it something, it must be first quality or some other quality, and unless it comes up to the standard that is set for first quality, then I think you are liable to a fine.

If you mark it second quality and it comes up to second quality, you would not be liable to a penalty. If you mark it first quality and it is found to be only second quality, then you are liable to a penalty. If you mark it XXX and it is found to be of a quality indicated by X or XX, then you would be liable to a penalty.

Section 4 provides that all fruit must be designated of some quality. Now, suppose a man marks his apples XX ; according * to this Bill it absolutely does not determine anything, because it might be precisely the same quality that is marked X by his neighbour, and the one not knowing at all how the other marked his apples. I would like to ask the hon. gentleman how it is possible to carry out the provisions of the Bill under such circumstances unless it is declared that there must be some mark specially indicating the quality. If that be the case then it is quite clear that punishments will be visited upon those who offend against the law. If you must have some mark and that mark means anything in most cases I do not see how it is possible to work that out.

That is just the object covered by section 8, and it is thought to be pretty completely covered by it as far as any definition of what we do not know can possibly do it. We do not know what marks different traders may put upon their fruit, but if any one puts a mark upon his fruit which appears to indicate that it is specially good and it is not so, section 8 would cover that :

whereas if we define only certain things as marks that were going to be covered by this Bill, then, anybody who did not put these marks upon his fruit, but who put other marks upon it intended to deceive, would not be liable to the penalties of the Bill. We think that section 8 covers that point.

I would suggest to the hon. minister to exempt from the operation of this law wild fruits, such as we have in the province of Quebec. There is no doubt that it is intended to apply particularly to garden-grown fruit.
Yes.

The possibility of applying the Bill to fruit grown in the fields or in the woods would be very great, and I would suggest to the hon. minister to exempt wild fruit entirely from the operation of the law.
What words would the hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk) suggest to cover that ?
I think the words * wild fruit ' in general would cover it.
Would the hon. gentleman's idea be covered by these words : ' Fruit not wild fruit ' in sections 6 and 7 ?
I think it, perhaps, may be made the subject of a special section, providing that fruit meant to be covered by this Act would not be meant to include wild fruit.

That is a new idea, but it is one, I think, well worthy of consideration. I think it would be a fair interpretation of the Bill, as my hon. friend has said. The full intention of the Bill was to deal with cultivated fruit. We can quite understand that wild fruit is much more difficult to grade than is cultivated fruit. I think, perhaps, that would completely cover the difficulty that has been raised this afternoon in regard to the change in these sections. If that is the feeling of the committee, I would be disposed to insert a clause saying that in this Bill the word ' fruit ' would not include wild fruit.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
I think the hon. minister should confine the Bill to apples and pears, as was originally intended. I do not see the object he has in introducing now the word ' fruits ' to take the place of ' apples and pears.' We do not know what trouble it will lead to. It has been suggested that it might apply to blueberries and cranberries, and he intends to except these, but the same objection will apply, perhaps, to some of the cultivated fruits that we purchase in closed packages. The whole discussion of the Bill was conducted the other

day upon the idea that it would apply to apples and pears. The hon. member tor South Wentworth (Mr. Smith), who takes a deep interest in the Bill, is not present today, and I would suggest, that, if the hon. minister is going on with the Bill, he should ask the committee to rise and report progress, and in the meantime that he should come to a conclusion as to what fruit the Bill should affect.

My hon. friend (Mr. Taylor) is entirely wrong in saying that the original intention of the Bill was that it should apply only to apples and pears. Sections 8 and 9, which are now in this reprinted Bill, and which were section 8 of the original Bill, as introduced in the committee the other day, distinctly applied to all kinds of fruit. My hon. friend has quoted the hon. member for Wentworth (Mr. Smith). The hon. member for Wentworth was a member of the committee of the Fruit Growers' Association which specially asked that this Bill should apply to other fruit than apples and pears, and that it should apply to the internal trade of the country instead of only to the export trade. The hon. member for South Leeds (Mr. Taylor), in saying that the original idea was that the Bill should apply only to apples and pears, is entirely wrong, and the quotation he has made is a misplaced one, inasmuch as he has not understood the views or wishes of the hon. member for Wentworth. The Bill certainly is desired and called for by the consuming public of the country to apply to other fruits besides apples and pears, and I think the advantages of the Bill would be extremely limited and largely minimized were it not to apply to all kinds of fruit. But, I must point out to the hon. gentleman that it is only when these other fruits are sold in closed packages that the Bill does apply to them. If they are sold in open packages, as' most of our small fruits are in this country, the Bill does not apply to them at all, and it does not create the difficulties which the hon. gentleman has mentioned. Is the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) writing a clause to cover the point which he mentioned ?
No, I am not ; but I will do so if the hon. gentleman wishes it.
I am quite willing to do it; I thought the hon. gentleman was doing it.

The more discussion that takes place the plainer is the need shown that we should define what is fruit. If you say ' wild fruit,' you may refer to an article that would be regarded as tame fruit in some cases. Take cranberries, for instance ; they are being planted in marshes and cultivated. They are wild fruit in one sense and tame fruit in another sense. They are largely gathered in the Georgian Bay district by the Indians. They are usually put up in barrels, and they would undoubtedly come under this Bill, unless you define what is meant by the word ' fruit.' Blueberries are treated in very much the same way. Sometimes they are put up in pails and sometimes in kegs. Apricots; and plums are also put up in barrels and kegs, so that all this fruit would come under this Bill. There is no doubt about that, and I think it would be much more workable and much more easily understood if you would insert a clause defining what is the meaning of the word ' fruit ' in this Bill, and stating to what fruit the Bill shall apply.

I think, as I expressed myself before, that if you begin to define the various kinds of cultivated or wild fruits you are going to get into no end of trouble. I do not think that anybody looks upon cranberries as cultivated fruit. They are looked upon simply as wild fruit, and they are so classed commercially. Take blueberries ; they are looked upon as wild fruit also, so that if you begin to enumerate what are wild fruits and what are cultivated fruits, you will get into no end of difliculty. If you accept the common-sense commercial term as to what are wild and what are tame fruits, you will be safe. You cannot begin to define what may be wild or what may be tame or cultivated fruits, and if you take the ordinary commercial acceptation of the term, there will be no difficulty.

If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Holmes) had been at the Agricultural Committee a few years ago, he would have heard one of the members of the staff giving information as to how they plant and cultivate cranberries in the maritime provinces. People there grow as many as fifty acres in a season, and they make a regular practice of raising them for sale. Would that not be regarded as tame fruit ? They are cultivated the same as tame fruit. If we specify the varieties of fruit that the Bill should apply to, then all others are outside of the operation of the Bill. The hon. gentleman speaks of the ordinary commercial term ' fruit,' but we do not know what it is. There may be the ordinary commercial term for cranberries, but who is to say whether it is tame fruit or wild fruit ? He may say it is wild fruit, and I may say it is tame fruit. Therefore, there is the difficulty to commence with. We can avoid that by specifying what is to be included urfder the operation of the Bill.
I understand the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) to say that in his section plums are shipped in barrels ?
Sometimes they are packed in barrels.

I represent a section of Ontario which produces a large quantity

of plums, and I never knew a barrel of plums to be skipped.

There is a great deal going on in the world that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Holmes) never knew of. I make the statement which I know to be a fact. It does not necessarily follow that because the hon. gentleman does not know it. nothing of the kind could occur.

I cannot see any great difficulty in designating the fruits that this Bill will cover. I cannot see how it is going to lead to such a lot of trouble as the hon. member for West Huron (Mr. Holmes) anticipates in his imagination. In my mind it would be a very simple thing to designate the fruit intended to be covered by this Bill. It need not take a very long clause to designate what you intend to cover by this Bill, and then all that is not named in this Bill would be outside of it and the Bill would not apply to it. That would be the simplest way out of it. If you name the fruits it will make your Bill workable and there will be no ' if ' about it.
I cannot see the object of giving a list of the fruits when it is fully intended that all fruit which is packed in closed packages shall be included.
You do not include wild fruits.

With the exception of wild fruits. When cranberries are packed in barrels I do not see why they should not be subject to the provisions of this Bill. It is true there are wild cranberries and cultivated cranberries, just as there are wild strawberries and cultivated strawberries, and in Nova Scotia, for instance, there are more cultivated than wild cranberries put upon the market. The words ' wild fruit ' would not cover cultivated cranberries. I think if we make the exception for wild fruit, that is all that will be necessary. I consider that the insertion of a list of fruits in the Bill would lead to difficulty.

How could the minister tell whether cranberries are wild or cultivated, and that must be determined before this Bill is workable. Sometimes cranberries are frozen for transport, and at other times they are packed in during the warm season. There are high bush and low bush cranberries, both of which are packed in barrels, and sometimes when you open the package they are bruised. When they are bruised they would not come under the definition of a high quality of fruit as provided in this Bill.

It seem to me that if you stencil on the package the words * wild fruit ' you would have no trouble in getting over the difficulty, and I' be-Mr. HOLMES.
lieve it to be a wise distinction to .make. Every dealer in cranberries knows that when he gets cranberries from Cape Cod he gets cultivated cranberries, because the name of the grower is placed on the package. If you get cultivated cranberries from Nova Scotia the name of the grower is on the package also, and you know that they are cultivated, whereas if they are gathered in the marshes the name is not put on the packages, and you know they are wild. The words ' wild fruit ' stencilled on. the package would cover the whole ground.

I shall move an amendment to clause 3 in accordance with the view of the hon. gentleman from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk), but in the meantime we had better proceed with the other clauses of the Bill.
On section 8,
The word * first ' is a misprint here, and I move to substitute for it the word ' finest.'

I would like the minister to tell us if he can, what is the substantial difference between clause G and clause 8. In one clause you put the words ' A No. 1, Canadian,' which I take it includes finest, best or extra good quality, specified in the other clause.
Yes.
Then why repeat the same thing in section 8 ?

Section 8 applies to other brands of a similar character which are not included in ' A No. 1, Canadian.' Section 8 would apply to superior or super-excellent or XXX, which a dealer might put upon his packages but not ' A No. 1, Canadian.'

The minister is quite mistaken. The sections are precisely the same except in one case you put ' A No. 1, Canadian,' which means finest, best or extra good quality, as the hon. gentleman admits. As a layman, I am perfectly amazed at the suggestion of the minister that there is any difference between the two. You simply say the same thing in different words. ,

Will the hon. minister give us a- full account of the requirements under this head, also the amount expended last year and the policy pursued. Will he please state whether these rails were bought by tender, and what the price was.

I may say that the amount here asked for is not likely to be all that we shall ask for this session, so the hon. gentleman must keep that fact in view. The hon. gentleman's (Mr. Hag-gart's) request is a very reasonable one, and I shall endeavour to give the information. Last year the rails were purchased by tender. They were furnished by two firms, a part by each-the Illinois Company and the Cambria Company. We had offers from these companies lower than those of others, including English manufacturers. The rails procured last year were to re-rail, as far as they would go, the Cape Breton line. We had some difficulty owing to the scarcity of labour last year and did not succeed in getting the whole ninety-four or ninety-five miles from Point Tupper to Sydney laid. I think we laid some seventy odd miles. The balance of the work we expect to complete as soon as the season will permit. The price we paid last year was $32.60 a ton. The arrangement made this year for the rails we propose to lay down during the next year, that is after 1st July, we pay for at the same price, $32.60. These rails we get in accordance with an arrangement entered into by the government, after consideration of the whole question, with the Sault Ste. Marie Power Company. We had a proposition from them to put in a steel rail plant to manufacture these rails in Canada. They satisfied us of their ability to do this work, and that they would be capable of establishing a very efficient plant, using ores of a superior quality. They said the steel which would be made from it would contain a percentage of nickel, which would be found in the rails they would make for us. Although this formed no element in the price, it would add materially to the durability and value of the rails, and we felt that that was an additional inducement for us to make the arrangement with them. The establishment of this industry was contingent upon their securing from the government a fair order, one sufficiently large to guarantee them employment for their factory-a basis, as it were, upon which to invite and encourage the introduction of capital for that purpose. As the government viewed the matter, it was one which we felt would appeal very strongly to the sympathetic consideration of the Canadian people. It would result in the establishment of a permanent industry and would secure to railway companies and others who might require rails, a supply obtainable in this 835
country, while giving employment directly and indirectly to a large number of people. While conferring an enormous benefit upon a very great public work, we would be at the same time conferring additional and important advantages on the country in an industrial sense. We made such an arrangement with them. In the first place the question came up in the form of a proposal. The company offered to undertake the manufacture and delivery of these rails lat such a price as similar rails of equal standard could be obtained in the open market. At the time we made these arrangements we instituted inquiries as to the current price of rails, and we found it would be impossible for us to place orders at that time for a delivery earlier than the fall of the present year, and that the prices obtainable would be at all events equal to the prices that we were paying last year, and which we had contracted for the year before. When we had assured ourselves with reference to what would be a reasonable price to pay, we made a contract with this company to deliver 25,000 tons of the quality and standard which we have been placing upon the road, a rail eighty pounds in weight, and we were to pay them $32.50 per ton, the delivery to commence in the first week in August, and to continue at such a rate that we would be able to lay the rails before the snow fell.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS (Hon. A. G. Blair).

speechtext: Where were they to be delivered ?

They were to be delivered to us in Montreal-that is in the present year. We have no permanent and explicit contract with them for the future, although in their proposal they asked us to give them a contract for a term of five years, and to give them an order for 50,000 tons with which to commence their industry. We finally concluded to give them an order for 25,000 tons, and while we have no explicit contract with them for any term beyond the year in which we are now entering, we have an understanding with them under which, if they furnish us, as they engage to do, with rails of the quality and standard we require, and at the current price in the English market, we are prepared to continue to take our rails from them.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Do I understand the minister that these rails are to be manufactured at the Soo ?

Yes. The plant is now under way. speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.
