In this case capital has provided rails weighing 56 lbs. to the yard, and it is the duty of income to maintain that 56 lbs. afterwards. Under the system adopted by the Minister of Railways he not only escapes the maintenance of that 56-lb. rail, but he is actually getting new rails instead of the old ones out of capital, and that has also the effect that his working expenses in the future are going to be improved at the expense of capital. Instead of being subject to this expense of maintenance year after year he is getting rid of the old rails and getting new ones in their places. He is getting 80-lb. rails as new material, and for several years his working expenses would be cut down by reason of these new rails being charged to the debt of the country. And why does the Minister of Railways do that ? Simply in order that he may make a good showing on his working expenses and on the management of his railway. No railway in the country would ever think of keeping its books in that way. You could never get the Grand Trunk Railway or the Canadian Pacific Railway to make such charges to capital account. If they did, the managers of those companies every few years could add a few pounds to the weight of the rails, and they would never spend a cent for maintenance except the mere cost of relaying. Now, I am' not trying to teach the minister (Hon. Mr. Blair) anything. He understands the matter perfectly well. I simply point out to the committee that the duty of the Minister of Railways is to maintain that 56 lbs. out of his income, less the value of the scrap, and the ouly thing he can properly charge to capital is the extra weight of the rail he puts in.
Will the hon. gentleman (Mr. Barker) just follow me for a moment. We have taken up the old Cape Breton rail which was a second-hand rail when put down
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Was not the Cape Breton rail used on the Intercolonial Railway before? I thought that only a part of them were taken up and replaced on the Intercolonial Railway by others, and that a great portion of them were new rails?

What difference would it make if they were used on another part of the Intercolonial Railway and transferred I to the Cape Breton Railway. It is all gov-

eminent railway, and they were new rails when originally put down.

They were inferior rails when they were put down in Cape Breton, and being old rails when they were put dowu they were practically of little more value than they were when they were taken up last year and when they are now being taken up, and when there are 80-lb. new rails substituted for them.
Mr. CLANCY! Does the hon. gentleman mean that they were old rails when originally purchased and put down, or that they were originally put down as new rails, and afterwards removed from one part to another ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: What I state, from information received from my officers, is, that they were old rails when put down on the Cape Breton line. The hon. gentleman would like me to charge them up as new and good rails, of equal quality of new rails of the same weight, although the late government transferred them from one portion of the line to another. I do not think that is a fair or reasonable proposition. We are charging simply the difference between their value as old rails and the value of new 80-pound rails.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I understand the hon. gentleman to mean that the bookkeeping should be affected by the fact that my hon. friend from Lanark (Hon. Mr. Hag-gart) happened to be the Minister of Railways at that time, while the hon. gentleman happens to be Minister of Railways at this time. If my hon. friend from Lanark were the Minister of Railways now, it would hardly be possible to carry out logically the suggestion which the hon. gentleman makes.

Then, with reference to the 66-pound rails which have been taken up, they are comparatively new rails-as good 56-pound rails as you could probably buy in the market to-day; and on any view that could be taken of the question, I do not think there could be the slightest criticism of the method in which these rails are being treated. They are good rails, and we are treating them as good rails; and they are being put down on the Prince Edward Island road at the same value at which they are being taken up from the main line of the Intercolonial Railway, the difference only being charged.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Do all the rails purchased this year, and last year and the year before, go into the store account-the gross quantity purchased or delivered; and is it then charged out ?

The Deputy Minister tells me | Mr. WALLACE.
that the new rails that have been purchased in times past go into the store account when they are being charged as against revenue. If you buy a large quantity of rails and keep them on hand, and they continue on hand for a term of years, they necessarily go into store account, and are only charged up when laid on the road.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: In other words, all the rails you purchased this year and last year and the year before that have not gone into store account at all, but are all charged to capital ?
That is correct.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Did I understand the minister to say that second-hand rails which had been placed on the Cape Breton road and used there are now being taken to Prince Edward Island and used for the construction of roads there ?

No, I did not say that. The hon. gentleman quite misunderstood me. I said that we are putting down on the Prince Edward Island road a very superior 59-pound rail, which has been a very short time in use. These rails are taken from the Drummond County Railway, which hon. gentlemen who have followed the discussions with regard to that road know is a road of recent construction. The rails put down on the Prince Edward Island road, if the hon. gentleman has seen them and knows anything about rails, he will say are very excellent rails.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Wrhen I had control of the Intercolonial Railway, there were a certain number of miles of railway to be renewed every year, and the rails used for this purpose were always charged to income. These never went into store account. The hon. gentleman has charged the full amount of the renewal of the road to capital account. While on my feet, I would like the hon. minister to tell me what English companies competed for these rails, and the prices they asked. I would also ask him whether he has any assurance that the smelting works will be built at Sault Ste. Marie in time to deliver the rails or any of them next fall ?

I cannot from memory tell the hon. gentleman the names of the English companies that tendered, but I will get the information. I remember that the price was $32.75 per ton, and that there were eight or ten firms tendering. I think they must have had a tacit understanding among themselves, for I think, though I would not he positive on the point, that most of the tenders were at the same figure.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Where was the delivery to take place ?
I think at Montreal.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Did the manufacturers pay the duty ?

They were not to have paid any duty on the rails. All the tenders we invited on the basis of price free of duty. With regal'd to the manufacture of rails at Sault Ste. Marie, I can only tell the hon. gentleman that before we placed this sum in the estimates, we had a communication with the company. We asked them not to mislead us in any way,' but to let us know with absolute confidence whether we could count on receiving the rails or any portion of them in the time specified.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: When was the contract made ?

Last fall or early in the winter. The proposition was laid before us, before the last session of parliament. We were not able to give it consideration while parliament was in session, but immediately after the session and as soon as we could, we opened up negotiations and came to an understanding with the company. Just what that date was I am not at the moment able to say.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman have the contract and those tenders immediately after dinner.

I do not know whether I correctly understood the hon. minister that these rails, when used for a new siding, were charged to capital account, but when they were put on an old siding they were charged to current account ?
If we were simply renewing work which had been done before, that would be charged against current account.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Does the hon. minister not see that these rails are twice charged to capital account ? When purchased originally, they were charged to capital account, and when put down on a new siding they are again charged to capital account ? It seems to me it demoralizes the bookkeeping badly.
How does the hon. gentleman get credit for the $15 old rails that go into the store account, when all the rails that are purchased and laid on the road never enter the store account at all ?
When the hon. gentleman gets old rails into sidings, at what rate does he charge out the rails-at scrap rate, $15 a ton ?
Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Is the hon. gentleman certain about that, because some of the items seem to indicate otherwise ?

Certainly. We might let this item stand, Mr. Chairman.
Railways and Canals-Chargeable to Capital- Railways-Intercolonial Railway-To complete highway bridge at Rocky Lake, $3,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: This will complete the expenditure of $8,000 for the purposes of diverting the highway and avoiding three existing dangerous level crossings. My hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Borden) knows the location of this work.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: That is between Windsor Junction and Halifax ? I know that there are dangerous level crossings there.
Why do you charge a highway bridge to capital account on a road finished so long ago as that between Windsor and Halifax ?

This is an entirely new bridge. It would be as reasonable not to charge any portion of the Intercolonial Railway to capital account, as to say that when you are going to make the road additionally safe by means of an entirely new structure you cannot properly charge it to capital.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: This is a new principle.

No. Here are three dangerous crossings on the level. It is desirable in the interests of the public that these dangerous crossings should be done away with. We make a diversion of the road and put in a new bridge, and we think we are fairly entitled to charge it to capital.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: You do not charge the diversion, but only the bridge to capital.

That is as I understand it, but I am not sure. No, I see I was wrong, and that the whole work, including the diversion, is charged to capital.
Railways and Canals-Chargeable to Capital- Railways-Intercolonial Railway-To build new and enlarge old engine houses, $75,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: What is this ?

Last year we appropriated $140,000 for this purpose. We have not yet expended the whole of that amount, but it will be expended by the end of the fiscal year. The works are estimated to cost $215,000, so that we are asking for the balance of what will be needed. This will enlarge some of the existing houses to ac-

commodate the larger engines, and we also propose to build new engine houses at places where they are needed.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: How many new ones ?
We are building new ones at Chaudiere and Stellarton.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: How many new engines does the hon. minister propose to accommodate ?
By the end of the current year we shall have at least eighty-five new engines of the 82-ton size.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: But the hon. gentleman has only increased the number by about twenty in the last three or four years.

Yes, but I have sixty-six under contract. We are enlarging the buildings at Campbellton, Ste. Flavie and Sydney. We are also lengthening the stalls at other engine houses, concerning which I have not the minute details at hand.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: What do the new engine houses cost ?
The engine house at Chaudiere will cost $60,000, and that at Stellarton between $55,000 and $60,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: This represents an expenditure of only $120,000, and the balance of this $215,000 will be consumed in repairing other engine houses ?
In enlarging and adding to them. For instance, I have seen the work in progress at Campbellton. We are taking out the wall, adding to the building and extending the pits and tracks.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Is all this work being done by tender ?
Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: How many stalls are being added at each place where enlargement is made ?
The number varies from fifteen to twenty-five-perhaps twenty would be the average.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The hon. gentleman does not propose to add as many as twenty at each place ? I am asking about those that are to be enlarged.
I am speaking of the ones enlarged.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Is it not possible to give the exact number in each case ?
That could be given, but I have not the information here.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I happened to be in the railway roundhouse at Truro a little while before coming here, and I saw one of these fine new engines, being moved on the turntable, and it looked very much as if the whole thing would break down. The workmen said, that an accident, accompanied with great loss of property, might occur any day ; because the engines were so much larger than the turntable was originally constructed to handle. I would ask the hon. gentleman to give this matter his attention, because if one of these turntables, should break down, the loss of public property would be far greater than the cost of renewing the table. We should have a new roundhouse, with all modern equipments, at Truro. I earnestly call the Ministers attention to this state of affairs.

What the hon. gentleman says is entirely correct, and it is the same ail over the line. When we are changing from a forty and forty-five and fifty ton engine to an eighty-two ton engine, you can well imagine there would be risks. The officers of my department and myself are fully sensible of the importance of having our turntables enlarged, and our engine houses enlarged as rapidly as possible. We are doing that as rapidly as we can, and Truro is not being overlooked.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Do you contemplate Truro in this present vote ?
I think there will be something in the supplementaries.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Will the minister bring down after dinner information in detail of this large expenditure ?
The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS >,ND CANALS. I can give the hon. gentleman 'the details now, except in respect to the stalls. But I do not think that we have had from the engineers any memo, of the plans of the different engine houses. At Stellarton the engine house is estimated to cost $58,500, and a turntable, $9,500. The Campbellton engine house is costing $25,000: the engine house at St. Flavie is estimated to cost $25,000 ; that at Sydney, $75,000 ; that at Chaudiere, $60,000. The enlargement of the stalls in other engine houses is put down at $12,000. I can get the information in respect to the stalls if the hon. gentleman desires it.
Increased accommodation at Sydney, $100,000.

The hon. gentleman will remember that I included in the first amount $25,-

2G46-
000 for the Sydney engine house. When that estimate was sent forward we were providing for six stalls in that engine house; after that came, it was found necessary to increase the number and we are putting in twelve additonal stalls in the Sydney engine house, the cost of which forms a portion of the present amount of $100,000. These additional stalls, boiler, engine house and foundations, will cost $50,000 in addition to the $25,000 that has already been asked for in a previous vote. Then we have to lay out a yard, and prepare grounds and tracks, all of which will cost $50,000 more.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Has there been any arrangement made with respect to running passenger trains into Sydney and North Sydney other than that which has hitherto prevailed ? There was a good deal of dissatisfaction in one of the towns, at least, with respect to the delay which took place.

We are about getting out time tables, and when the new time table comes out we expect finally to settle that question, which has given rise, I think, to a good deal of unreasonable controversy, though there may be a difference of opinion. It is not to be wondered at that the people of Sydney complained of the delay in the arrival of trains by reason of their being shunted off to North Sydney. I think I stated last year that my own view was that such a condition ought not to continue ; and I think we will be able to give a service to both Sydney and North Sydney which will be satisfactory to all concerned.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Sydney is where the steel works are being erected ?
Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: As it is nearly six o'clock, I will remind the hon. minister of the notice that I put upon the paper some time ago for the purpose of eliciting information from the Railway Department that we would like to get very much for the purpose of discussing the state of affairs on the Intercolonial Railway. Among the payments is a sum of $4,527,807, including railway and canal collections. Now, I want a separate statement of the canal collections from the railways. The notice has been on the paper for ten days, and the minister has been promising to get the information day after day. Then there is a sum here of the receipts and payments of canals, this is the ten-days' statement. There is the railways and canals consolidated fund of $118,972, I would like to know what constitutes that item. I suppose that nothing of capital account appears in this statement at all.

I am not able to separate The canal collections from the railway collections this evening, but we will not get
through these railway estimates to-night, and my hon. friend will have another opportunity "of getting this information placed in his hands, and he will have another chance to discuss it.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I suppose the hon. gentleman is going to make a statement of his whole management of the Intercolonial Railway, and I would like to have this information before he makes that statement. He will find the question was put on March 29th by my hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker).

I rememb'er that the question came up, and I was obliged to inform my hon. friend that I had not received the information from Moncton, but the deputy minister informs me that it will be ready to-morrow.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Are tenders let for these improvements that are going on under contract ?	.
Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Does the minister include-in these contracts the current wage clause as a specification 1

Well, I do not think it has been customary on the Intercolonial Railway. We have not yet met with any difficulty at aii except this, that probably the general effect of what has taken place in parliament and out of parliament in regard to wages has added quite a material amount to the cost of labour 1 do not say I regret that, nor do I say that it ought not to have been so, but that has been the effect. We have not found it necessary to include any clause in our contracts in order to secure the payment of a proper and reasonable wage.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The hon. minister will remember that the resolution passed by this House last year called for its application to all government works, and surely a contract of this kind must be considered a government contract, even although it is on the Intercolonial Railway. It seems to me that it should be included, and as the hon. minister admits that the cost of labour has already been increased it will not further increase the cost.

It is not a very easy thing, if I may remind the hon. gentleman, with the multiplicity of small contracts we are making on the Intercolonial Railway to carry out his wish. We would have to make a very considerable addition to our working staff in order to pursue these details, and unless there was some good reason for taking on this additional burden we would not feel like doing it. We would not want

to incur that expense. I am quite sure tliat if there had been any ground for complaint at all in reference to the amount of wages that is being paid we would have heard of it. I do not find that the people are at all slow in making such things known to the department. We have never heard anything of that kind in reference to the contracts we have made. These contracts are small matters, and you would encumber them very much.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
They may be small matters, although the items are not very small. I do not think this would increase the cost of the Railway Department at all. We have a Labour Department now. We are going to be asked to vote $50,000 for that department, and we should give the department something to do. I think the Labour Department could take hold of this matter.
At six o'clock, the committee took recess.
After Eecess.
Committee resumed at eight o'clock.
Administration of Justice-Miscellaneous expenditure, including North-west Territories. $37,000.
What is this miscellaneous expenditure ? I see the amount is exactly the same as last year.

This Is the customary amount for federal purposes, and includes fees in the North-west Territories for Crown prosecutors, sheriffs, clerks of the court, maintenance and transport of prisoners, coroners' inquests, copies of evidence in applications for executive clemency and general expenditures of that description in the North-west Territories, and also here at headquarters.
What was the expenditure last year ?

The total amount voted was expended.
Travelling allowances, court of King's Bench and county court judges, Manitoba, $3,000.
There is an increase here.
There is an increase of $500, because the amount of $2,500 voted last year proved to be inadequate. An increase is asked for because of the increased business in Manitoba.
Would this represent the travelling expenses or allowance for judges on circuit ?
The judges receive a per diem allowance of $6. This is not an exorbitant charge when you consider expenses in that part of the country. Circuit allowances to judges ad hoc, $200.
What is the occasion of payments to judges ad hoc ?

In the event of a judge being disqualified in any district, or in the event of not being able, to have a judge to send on circuit. They send a judge out specially for the purpose of taking a case in which the judge would be disqualified.
Is this restricted to any province or is it applicable to the Dominion as a whole ?

I am not able to say where that expenditure was made last year, but I do not anticipate that it is applicable to any particular province. I cannot say whether it was expended last year or whether any portion of it was expended.

I know that in my own province sometimes a county court judge is disqualified and a judge from another district comest to take his place, but, I supposed that would be dealt with as a circuit allowance for a county court judge.
In the province of Quebec that is the way it is dealt with. I have no present recollection of that particular item or as to the purposes for which it is expended. It is only a matter of $200.
Has it been expended ?
I am not able to say whether it was expended last year or not. I am quite willing to allow that item to stand if hon. gentlemen desire it.
I do not think the hon. gentleman need let it stand, but he may mention it again.

I find here a memorandum which says that this vote is occasionally required, but it has not been drawn on this year.
To provide for the enforcement of the Alien Labour law, $9,000.
How is that vote used ?

Up to the present, a very small proportion of this item has been expended. Hitherto the administration of the Alien Labour Act has been in charge of the Department of Justice, but now it has been transferred to the Postmaster General, and it will be for him to explain in the future how this vote is used.
Did it cost us $9,000 last year ?
It only cost us $966.66.

I would rather be inclined to think that a smaller vote would be required than formerly, for the reason that under the new legislation the enforcement of this Act is left to private

individuals in the provinces, under the sanction of the provincial Attorney General, or of a judge. I do not at present quite see the necessity for so large a vote, but I would not feel inclined to say that this amount should not be voted if the Solicitor General will tell us that it reasonably might be required.

I did not understand from the Bill introduced the other day that the law would be left entirely to the initiative of private individuals. They would put the law in motion, but I am not quite sure that to a large extent the government may not be responsible for expenditure connected with the administration of the law as heretofore.

It is quite true there is nothing in the Bill to prevent the government from proceeding to enforce the law, but, on the other hand, there is nothing in the Bill which would enable the government to indemnify a private prosecutor who acted on his own responsibility.
Judging from the experience of the past, I do not think it likely all this money will be used, but, at all events, it cannot do any harm to place a sufficient sum at our disposal.

Unless the government show greater alacrity in enforcing the law in the future than in the past, a couple hundred dollars would be sufficient.
Penitentiaries generally, $3,560.
What is the increase of $160 for ?

There is an annual increase of $30 in the salary of the stenographer, and $130 for office contingencies. This is the first increase in this item that has taken place during six years.
Kingston penitentiary, $190,500.

There is an increase of $100 to provide for an assistant for the farm instructor, the extent of the farm having been increased by fifty acres last year.
St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary, $111,700.

I would like to ask the Solicitor General if he knows whether the two guards who were found guilty of an assault on the ex-warden are still in the employ of the government ? I may mention that during the last election five of these guards, in a -premeditated manner, arranged to assault the ex-warden after a political meeting, and pursuant to that arrangement did assault him. The ex-warden was very seriously hurt. They were brought before a magistrate and were found guilty, or pleaded guilty to aggravated assault, and subsequently they withdrew their plea. They were taken before another magistrate, and two of them were found guilty of simple assault. The whole affair was very unsatisfactory, but what I wonder is, if these two guaTds, who were condemned to a fine, have been dismissed from the service. I may tell the Solicitor General that during the past election many of the employees of the St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary were actively engaged in the work of the election. I saw some of them myself at political meetings, but the case of these two guards is one which deserves special attention.

I am not in a position to say whether the two guards referred to have been dismissed. My present opinion is that they have not been ; that they paid the fine to which they were condemned. With regard to the charge that the people of St. Vincent de Paul took part in the election, I know nothing about it ; but, I would accept the word of my hon. friend (Mr. Monk) when he says he knows it of his own knowledge. I am afraid, however, that that is a tradition of long standing at St. Vincent de Paul, and it should be made to disappear.

It is quite possible it has existed in the past, but the Solicitor General should see that some kind of check should be put upon it in the future.
Dorchester penitentiary, $54,500.
What is the explanation of this increase of $900 ?

It is to provide for a masonry instructor, whose salary will be $700, and the other $200 is for that amount under-estimated last year.
Regina jail, $10,600.
There is an increase here of $1,100.

There is an increase in salaries of $500, which has become necessary to provide for a night engineer; an increase in the maintenance of prisoners of $300, due to an increase in the price of beef and other provisions; and an increase of $300 in working expenses.
Administration of justice in the Yukon territory-Additional salary of judge, $1,000.
If you paid the judge $4,000 before, why should he get $5,000 now ?

The experience we have had during the last two years has led to the conclusion that the salaries of the officials in the Yukon are too low to enable them to live even in moderate comfort, and it is proposed to allow the judges $5,000 a year each, with $250 a month for living allowance, and the sheriff and clerk of the court $3,000 a year each, with $150 a month for living allowance. My hon. friend will realize that $5,000 a year to a judge of the high court in the Yukon, who is called upon to administer the laws and decide matters of very great importance, is not ex-I orbitant. It is the salary paid to the high

court judges In Ontario and the superior court judges in Quebec.	*
Why do you have the words ' authorized by statute ' attached to the vote of the salary of one judge, and not to the other ?
Because there is provision made by the statute for only one judge. A vote was taken last year for an additional judge.
Under what authority was the second judge appointed ?
Under the authority of the vote in the estimates. If the salary is provided, the judge can be appointed.
If a statute creates a court and authorizes one judge, I do not suppose you would appoint another judge simply by voting a salary to him ?
The statute provides for the appointment of one or more judges. Therefore the statutory salary is for one, and then we vote an additional salary for the other.
Then I understand that the authority for the appointment of the second judge was statutory.

I do not wish to complain at all of the increase of salary for the Yukon judges, because I have no doubt that the conditions of life change there ; nor do I wish to reopen the question of the salaries of other judges, because that has already been fully treated in the House. But I would like to ask the Solicitor General if the government have under consideration, with the hope of any prompt solution, the question of a readjustment of the salaries of the judges of the province of Quebec. The Solicitor General is well aware that the judges of the city of Montreal are admittedly underpaid; and if changed conditions in the Yukon necessitate an increase, the conditions in the city of Montreal changed long ago, and the present salaries of the judges there are totally insufficient. I understand that the judges in the city of Toronto have grants of some kind from the local legislature, which bring their remuneration up to $1,000 over the remuneration of the judges in the same position in the city of Montreal.
They have other advantages also.

The members of the bar who know the situation of the judges in the city of Montreal, and the great increase in the cost of living there, know that their position is rapidly becoming intolerable. They cannot move in the matter, and that makes it all the more the duty of those who see what they go through to bring the matter to the attention of the proper authorities.

I may say that speaking in another place, the Minister of Justice stated that he had then under consideration a Bill to provide for increasing the salaries of the judges throughout the country. Speaking for myself, and judging from the work done by the judges in the province of Quebec, they are all undoubtedly underpaid for the services they perform. The comparison with the province of Ontario is to the disadvantage of our judges ; but that is a matter over which we have absolutely no control, because the local legislature provides that the judges shall receive $1,000 a year each, in addition to their salaries, until such time as their salaries shall be increased by the Dominion to $6,000, when the allowance of the province shall cease. Personally I think the salaries of the judges throughout the whole Dominion of Canada ought to be increased.
Is the salary for the additional judge mentioned here authorized by statute ?

The appointment of both judges is provided for by statute.
Salary of sheriff of Yukon territorial court, in addition to such fees of office as may be allowed by the Governor in Council, $3,000.
Is there no tariff of fees for the sheriff except what is allowed him by the Governor in Council ?
Out of the fees they are allowed to take an amount sufficient to bring their net salary up to $4,000 after having paid certain amounts to their deputies.
There is $1,000 added. Then, will the fees which they are allowed to collect just make up the difference between that and $4,000 ?

There is a tariff of fees established in the Yukon as payable to sheriffs and other deputies, just as in the older provinces-not the same amounts, of course, but fixed. Out of the fees these officers receive, they are entitled to take a sum sufficient to make their salaries $4,000. They account for the balance, paying it over to the Yukon officials entitled to receive, or to the Receiver General.
Apparently, the additional fees have not been enough to make the salaries up to $4,000.
Up to the present time that is the case.

As to these living allowances-I thought that the salary of the judge was for him to live on, but I see he has a living allowance in addition to $3,000. Does the judge account for it in any way ? If his living expenses were only $500, would he be given the $3,000 ?

No. He renders an account to the department, which is vouched for by the officials of the department in accordance with the rules of the Auditor General's office. I may say that there is not a great deal left of the living allowance each year.
The conditions of the Yukon are greatly changed, are they not ? They tell me, that one can go there, in three or four days, from British Columbia. What makes living so expensive there ?
I have not been there recently, but I understand that it costs considerably more to live in the Yukon than to live in any other part of the Dominion.
But going to the Yukon is a mere pleasure trip now. There are a lot of people, in my own Province, who intend going there this summer, for a pleasure trip.
It may be delightful in the summer, but I am not sure that it would be the same in winter.

But the supplies are taken in, in the summer, when carriage is least expensive. It is no part of our training, in my part of the country, to haggle about these little matters. But I would rather see the $3,000 added to the judge's salary and be done with it.
Services in the Yukon Territory-Administration of Justice-Living allowances of sheriff and clerk of court, $1,800 each, $3,600.
Here is an increase of
The Intention Is to allow the sheriff and the clerk a living allowance. This is in accordance with the amount now paid to the officials in the territory, $150 a month.

As the hon. member for Colchester truly observes, we naturally suppose that the cost of living in the Yukon is growing less, becoming more like what it is in the older provinces. But these allowances are being Increased. Can the Solicitor General tell us the reason of that ?

Originally, when the officials were sent in, in 1897, a certain amount was allowed as living allowance. But it was afterwards found not at all sufficient to maintain them. The necessity for an increase has become apparent from actual experience. I think my hon. friends who are at all familiar with the Auditor General's administration may feel perfectly satisfied that there is nothing allowed to these officials to which they are not entitled. This is not a sum which they may have and dispose of as they please. They have to account for it. They make their claim, which is not allowed unless it
is established to the satisfaction of the Auditor General.
They seem like princely establishments.
I am not sure that there is anything princely about them.
Has the Solicitor General the date of the statute fixing the salaries for officers of the Yukon territorial court ?
It must have been 1897-1 will send for it.
Anything like a decent house in Dawson City will cost a rental of $2,000 a year.

I should like to have been informed of that before.
Services in the Yukon Territory-Administration of Justice-Maintenance of prisoners, $20,000.
On what system are the prisoners taken care of out there ?
Just as in the older provinces. Provision is made to give them what they are fairly entitled to as prisoners.
Has the Solicitor General any idea what it costs per capita ?
I did not think of making inquiry, and have not the information at hand. I could get the information.

I understood that in the past the expenses were very high, but I think no information has been given to the House on this subject on any previous occasion. It seems to me it would be a matter of some importance to have these facts.

I am satisfied, if my hon. friend wishes, to give that information on concurrence.
Services in the Yukon Territory-Administration of Justice-Transport of prisoners, $5,000.
This is altogether new, apparently.
This is intended to repay to the mounted police appropriation the sums paid for expenses incurred in moving prisoners from place of arrest to place of confinement.

Then, a similar reduction should be made in the mounted police estimates, as this seems to be a- matter of book-keeping. Can the Solicitor General tell us whether that appropriation has been reduced ?

I do not know. As I am informed, they return vouchers to the Department of Justice for this particular service, and we pay the amount. That would imply, as I understand

it, that there has been an increase in the expenditure of the mounted police.
But, if there is an increase here to repay an amount to the mounted golice, I should think there must be a corresponding reduction somewhere else.
Yes, if there was the same amount of work done.
In previous years, how was this charged ?
The work was not done, I presume, until quite recently, until the last year or so. This expenditure, I presume, has become necessary as the result of the settling of the country.
But, within the last year or two this must have appeared in the expenditure of the mounted police.

I apprehend that until it became a large amount they would pay it and not seek to be recouped by the Department of Justice. But, when it increased to so large an amount as $5,000, and as it is part of the administration of justice, they wish the Department of Justice to bear it. That is the explanation which suggests itself to my mind at present.
No doubt my hon. friend (Mr. Fitzpatrick) is right. Still, it would seem to me there should be a reduction of some amount of the estimates of the mounted police.
I would suggest that my hon, friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax) might hold that question over until the estimates of the mounted police are under discussion.
Does the hon. gentleman have charge of those estimates ?
No.
1 can see the reason why he wished to put it off on some one else. Who has charge of the mounted police ?
The Prime Minister.

Perhaps me right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) could tell ns about that ?

There is an increase here of $8,000.

Yes, the explanation I have is that last year the vote was $7,000, and it was reported by the judges and the Crown prosecutor as too small. I asked for information to enable me to estimate the amount accurately. I was told that they have not got at the pres-Mr. FITZPATRICK.
ent time in the Department of Justice sufficient data to estimate exactly the amount required. The amount asked for is largely tentative.
Is Mr. Wade the Crown prosecutor in the Yukon ?
I cannot say, but we do not address the Crown prosecutor in a matter of this kind.

Have the department changed their system, which prevailed some time ago, where the government prosecutor could at the same time do ordinary professional work, as Mr. Wade did, in connection with the vessel where he took a case for the prosecution and the same case for the defence ?
I think the Crown prosecutor would have the same privilege as in the other provinces. In Quebec the Crown prosecutor takes private practice as well as doing Crown business.

But the facts were stated in this House, and not denied, and I think they were substantiated. Out of the deposit that the owner of the vessel made as a guarantee that he would stand his trial, the Crown prosecutor took $700. At the same time he was giving the defendant advice, he was being paid a salary by the government.

The hon. gentleman is entirely mistaken. The charge, or the suggestion, was made by the hon. member for Pictou (Sir Charles Hibbert Tupper) in the House, that Mr. Wade had charged both sides of the case. I stated then I was perfectly satisfied that the statement was made without evidence of any kind. When Mr. Wade saw the report he telegraphed me a denial, and asked me to bring it up in the House.

What became of the man's money ? My remembrance of the statement made by the member for Pictou is, that out of the $900 deposited by the vessel-owner as a guarantee that he would stand his trial, $700 was retained by Mr. Wade.

I think every lawyer in the House will agree with me that the thing is so outrageous as to be incredible. In my experience I never heard of a lawyer even being charged with the offence. If there was the least possible doubt about it, I am sure the Department of Justice would have looked into it. All I remember is that the member for Pictou made the statement, and subsequently a telegram or a letter came from Mr. Wade positively denying it.

But, the statement was deliberately made in the presence of many members of this House, that the owner of the vessel went to Mr. Wade for advice, and received advice from him, regarding

the very case concerning -which Mr. Wade was advising the collector of customs who seized the vessel. That statement is in the ' Hansard.' The charge was made, whether the Minister of the Interior remembers it or not.

I remember the charge, but there was certainly no evidence.

I would like to ask the Solicitor General what position Mr. W. H. P. Clement occupies in the	Yukon territory ?
The	MINISTER	OP	THE	INTERIOR.
None at the present time. He resigned some time last summer.

He is not now in the employ of the government ?
The	MINISTER	OP	THE	INTERIOR.
No.

The criticism which my hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) referred to was made in the House last year. It was to the effect that while Mr. Wade was acting as legal adviser he was engaged in private practice. That was a thing that I do not- think the Minister of the Interior himself was much inclined to defend, because after the criticism was made upon it or before, he put a stop to it. It was a very bad thing, particularly under the peculiar conditions which existed in the Yukon at the time, that a lawyer should be advising the government and at the same time be at liberty to practice among individuals. However, the Minister of the Interior did stop it, but he should never have permitted it to begin. The other circumstance to which the member for Grey referred had something to do with the customs. According to my remembrance, the criticism was to the effect that Mr. Wade was acting for the collector of Customs and was also acting for one of the persons who had .some dispute before that collector.

A vessel came into port and was seized for violation of the customs law. The vessel-owner desired to take his vessel out within a few days, as otherwise it would be frozen in, and that would be a serious loss to him. He decided, to satisfy the officials that he would stand his trial, to put up a deposit, I think the amount was $900, if they would allow the vessel out so that he might get it away before the river froze over. The vessel was then released, but I believe was afterwards seized again. In the meantime, while Mr. Wade was giving advice to the collector of customs, the vessel-owner was getting advice from Mr. Wade as the defendant in the case ; and out of the deposit which was put up as a guarantee that he would stand his trial, Mr. Wade kept $700. If my memory is correct, Mr. Wade said that that was to pay for his charges in connection with the case, and the vessel-owner did not get it back.
Could the hon. gentleman tell me if the position Mr. Clement occupied was abolished, or was some person appointed in his stead ?
Mr. Connolly, of Halifax, was appointed in his stead.
What are the names of the two judges there ?
Judge Craig and Judge Dugas. Judge Dugas was appointed in 1897 or 1898, and Judge Craig was appointed last year.
I do not see any provision for their salaries under the Act.
I did not quite gather from the Solicitor General the reasons for the increase of $8,000 in this vote, more than 100 per cent.

The reason is based entirely upon the returns made by the judges and the Crown prosecutor of the district, namely, that the amount voted heretofore, $7,000, was entirely inadequate. At the same time, I have to admit to my hon. friend that we have not got sufficiently detailed information to enable us to say that $12,000 or $14,000 will be sufficient, and we are obliged to ask for $15,000 to meet the exigencies of the case.
How much was necessary last year ?

I cannot say, but we were $3,000 or $4,000 short last year.
Law books, &c., and freight thereon for the use of the bench and bar, and stationery and freight thereon for territorial court, $2,500.

The increase is made up by the enormous expenditure we have been obliged to make for freight. The greater portion of the money was used in paying freight charges. We have asked for $500 additional so that If possible we may have $2,000 free for the purchase of books.
Miscellaneous expenses, Including fees and expenses of Crown prosecutor, salaries and living allowances of stenographers for territorial a,nd police courts, and other officials or employees connected with the administration of justice, coroners' inquests, &c., &e., $30,000.

This is a very large increase, but it is caused by the fact that last year the amount was entirely insufficient. As a matter of fact last year a portion of the expenditure named in this item was met by the Interior Department. There are four stenographers, two for the high court and two for the police court. Each of these men receive $3,000, making over $10,000 for stenographers alone.
How much was expended last year ? The vote was $8,000.
I cannot say. '
Can you give us any idea ?
No, I cannot ; I am not in a position to tell you because the whole amount that was expended in excess was paid by the Interior Department.
Is this designed to cover what was expended by the Justice Department as well as by the Interior Department ?
No, it is designed to cover what ought to have been expended by the Justice Department, and which was expended in part by the Interior Department.
I have not the particulars here, but I can give them to the hon. gentleman to-morrow.
As this is a very large increase, perhaps the hon. Solicitor General would not mind allowing it to stand.
I am quite satisfied to allow it to stand.
I am not as familiar with the territorial court in the Yukon as I ought to be. I see you have two stenographers for the police court. Is that another name for the territorial court ?
You have the high court judges, and then in addition to that you have the police court.
Has It just the ordinary jurisdiction of a municipal court ?
The ordinary jurisdiction of a police court for the trial of summary cases.
What is the need of stenographers ? We do not have any stenographers in the eastern police courts.
We have them in many cases in our province. There are two in Montreal and one in Quebec.
Not in the police court.
My hon. friend will have to allow me to insist. I have been in the police court-not as a defendant-quite recently.
There is one in the criminal court and the court of sessions.
Investigations are taken down now in short hand.
Preliminary investigations.

All the preliminary investigations are taken down by stenographers ; at least that is when the magistrate desires it for the criminal court. There is one of these stenographers who takes evidence in the criminal court for the benefit of the judge.
In preliminary investigations.
It would be for preliminary investigations. There are two in Montreal and one in Quebec.
I am very glad to hear that you have all these luxuries. We will endeavour to imitate you.
I would like to remind the hon. gentleman (Mr. Gourley) that when he proceeds to imitate what we do in the Yukon it will be at the expense of his province.

I have now the item to which I referred, and I want to give a little of the information contained in 'Hansard' to satisfy the hon. Minister of the Interior that what I said had some foundation in fact. On a motion to adjourn Sir Charles Hibbert Tupper refers to the matter. He is speaking of Mr. D. W. Davis, collector of customs, and his conduct in connection with the seizure of the vessel called the Yukoner. He says :
He was asked, in compliance with the advice of the Department of Justice, to account for his conduct, to disgorge the money that he had taken out of the hands of a company doing business in the Yukon, instead of which he handed

it over to Mr. F. C. Wade, of exceptional notoriety, the gentleman who holds so many government offices, and in connection with these offices is able to obtain extraordinary treatment for his clients every time he has to deal with the government. A public company, owning the steamer ' Yukoner,' an English company, incorporated in London, sends that ship into Canadian waters. The law is violated time and again, according to the information that I have. The owners of the ship are wronged by Mr. D. W. Davis, and Mr. F. C. Wade is benefited by $750 of hard cash, actually wrung out of that company and put into the pockets of Mr. F. C. Wade. All that is disclosed by the papers.
He was trying to get more information in regard to this matter.
When these London capitalists seek the protection of the Canadian government against an officer of the Canadian government, whose action has been reported upon by the Department of Justice as high-handed and improper.
That is where he refers to the case. He is desiring to get more Information in regard to it, he has put his question on the paper, and they have refused to give him the information. He culls this from the report made by a government official to the Department of Justice, or through the Department of Justice, or through Mr. Ogilvie, in which he speaks of the action of Mr. Wade as high-handed and improper. This gentleman admits that he took $750 belonging to this English company, while at the same time he was advising the collector of customs what to do on the other hand. He was the adviser of the Crown as well as the adviser of the defendant in the case.

i do not know the merits of this discussion or what took place here last year, but, as a gentleman's name has been brought up in this discussion, I would like to say a word or two in regard to the matter. I have known Mr. E. C. Wade as a practitioner in the city of Winnipeg since 1882. There are about eighty lawyers practising in the city of Winnipeg, and I do not think there is one in the city more honourable or straightforward than Mr. Wade. There are two brothers of the hon. member for Pictou (Sir Charles Hib-bert Tupper), as well as Mr. Hugh John Macdonald practising there, and I do not know that any of these gentlemen will say that in eighteen years one dishonourable act was ever brought before any of the Judges in regard to Mr. Wade's manner of carrying on practise. As far as I can hear this was not a matter before a judge but a matter of arbitration. I submit that before the name of a lawyer of the good standing of Mr. Wade is discussed in this way, he should at least have an opportunity of giving an explanation in .some manner to this House.

The hon. gentleman should know that Mr. Wade was called upon to give an explanation, and that he 84*
practically said : ' It is none of your business.' It is a well-known fact that when he was acting as adviser to the collector of customs he advised him to make the seizure of this vessel. The owners of the vessel go to him for advice, he advises them to make a deposit with the collector of customs, they do so, and when the collector of customs is asked for that deposit he says that he paid it over to Mr. Wade as his fee. To say that Mr. Wade enjoyed an honourable reputation in the city of Winnipeg may be all right enough ; there is no person calling that in question, but that has no reference to an act that he did in another capacity, or to the fact that an official of this government reported that his conduct was high-handed and improper. Surely one who was sent to look into it ought to know a great deal more about it than the hon. gentleman who deigns to enlighten the House as to the character of Mr. Wade. It would be more becoming if we had some information or defence from either the Minister of the Interior or the Solicitor General, than from an hon. member who knows nothing about it.

do not think there is any defence required in regard to the matter. It was threshed out pretty well last session and the session before. The facts are, as 1 remember, that the vessel was seized in the Yukon by the collector of customs, because of a complaint made by the seamen that their wages had not been paid. The vessel was tied up to the wharf, and the owners contended the collector had no right to seize her. They laid a caveat against the seizure, and after some time an agreement was come to that the vessel should be allowed to proceed, the dispute to be referred to an arbitrator whose award should be accepted by both sides. The collector then released the vessel and a certain amount was paid by the owners into the hands of the collector to abide the result of the award. The collector handed over the money in pursuance of the award. After the award was made, the parties who represented the vessel attempted to revoke the submission, and the collector ignored their right to do so. That was the matter in controversy. The collector said he had released the vessel on their submission to arbitration, and that he would pay the money in pursuance of the award. Whether or not they had the technical legal right to revoke the submission I do not inquire, but on the justice of the case it did appear that the collector was justified in paying the money over. I speak with diffidence, because I only know the facts as they came out in the debate, but it seems to me that a mountain was made out of a molehill, and that so far as Mr. Wade is concerned he simply received the money from the collector for his services as counsel.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES. I.

speechtext: Counsel for whom ?
I do not know which side he was on.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: He was acting for the owners of the vessel, and he was acting for the government as well.

The government had nothing to do with this matter. The sailors filed their proper complaint and got the vessel seized. The Merchants Shipping Act provides that certain proceedings are to be taken, and when the vessel was tied up, rightly or wrongly, an agreement was come to and signed by the parties that the dispute should be referred to arbitration. I shall not discuss the legal right of one of the parties to revoke the submission, but it did seem to me that whatever complaint might be against Mr. D. W. Davis the collector, there was no ground of complaint against Mr. Wade, unless you prove that his charges were excessive, and I have never heard that contended.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I do not know that this has much to do with the item, but since the minister (Hon. Sir Louis Davies) has entered into a discussion, I may say that I do not think that the matter is so clear as he would lead us to believe. If the collector of customs was allowed to act the parts of Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde, it was a very simple thing indeed. According to the views the hon. gentleman (Hon. Sir Louis Davies) put forward last year, at one moment he was collector of customs, and Mr. Wade was consulted by him as such; the next moment he was not acting as collector, but as arbitrator.
I do not think he was the arbitrator.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
Oh, yes, my recollection is that he was the arbitrator. At one moment he was collector of customs and an officer of the government, and the next moment he was arbitrator, and then as soon as the money came to him-according to the statement of the minister last year-he came back to Dr. Jeykll again, and was collector of customs. It was perfectly absurd that he could be doing his duty in all these different capacities and that Mr. Wade could be advising him in one capacity and then in another and the crew of the ship as well, and be doing his, duty to his clients. That was the argument of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries last session. I do not know sufficient of the facts to cast any reflection on Mr. Wade, but I do say that the matter was not explained to my satisfaction last year. I do not say that there is not a reasonable explanation of it, but I was not able to get any explanation last year to satisfy me, although the Minister Sir LOUIS DAVIES.
of Marine and Fisheries exerted to the utmost his well-known powers for the purpose of making it perfectly plain that there was no ground for criticism at all.
I think the charge was against Davis and not against Wade.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: The charge was against the collector of customs. The criticism that was made on the collector was that he went as such to Mr. Wade because Mr. WTade was the Crown prosecutor, or the solicitor recognized by the government as having a standing there; and then, when this matter was dealt with by that same collector of customs as an arbitrator, Mr. Wade appeared for one of the parties before him. That was the criticism upon Mr. Wade's position. . Whether there is any thing in it or not I do not know.
I think that was it.
