There is also a matter which the senior member for Pictou (Sir Charles Hibbert Tupper) mentioned to me before he left. It is with regard to an appeal from the high court of the Yukon territory. I understood from the Minister of the Interior that that appeal was to be confined to the Supreme Court of the province of British Columbia, and I want to know from the Minister of the Interior whether or not he has taken into consideration the advisability of having an appeal-either a further appeal or an alternative appeal-to the Supreme Court of Canada. Speaking without very much knowledge of the class of litigation which might be dealt with on such an appeal it would seem to me that 'the magnitude of some of the cases which probably would arise there would justify either an alternative appeal or a further appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada. A precedent can be found for that in the statute which deals with the admiralty jurisdiction of the Exchequer Court. From the local judge of the Exchequer Court sitting in admiralty an appeal may be taken either to the judge of the Exchequer Court at Ottawa, or to the Supreme Court of Canada; and if the appeal is taken in the first instance from the local judge to the judge of the Exchequer Court, then a further appeal may be taken from him to the Supreme Court of Canada. It seems to me that the Minister of the Interior may very well take into consideration as to whether some such scheme as that is not necessary in view of the magnitude of causes which probably arise in the Yukon territory. As to whether or not suitors in those courts should not have the benefit of an appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada, as suitors in other provinces have with respect to litigation involving very trifling amounts, I would be glad to have an expression of opinion from the hon. gentleman.

I did not catch the first remarks of my hon. friend, and I thought they applied to appeals in mining cases, but my hon. friend the Solicitor General says the leader of the opposition refers to appeals In ordinary civil cases.

I was referring to cases which were dealt with by the Minister of the Interior when he made a statement to the hon. member for Pictou
the other day in the House. I am not very familiar with the jurisdiction of the courts in the Yukon. I suppose there is an appeal in ordinary cases to the Supreme Court of Canada, is there not ?
To the Supreme Court of British Columbia.

If there is not an appeal from the Yukon court to the Supreme Court of Canada at present, I would extend my remarks to that. I think the magnitude of many mining claims would justify a further appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada-at all events, an alternative appeal.

The jurisdiction which the Minister of the Interior has officially in regard to mining claims arose under the mining regulations, and has gone on for a considerable number of years. As I explained to the House in answer to the hon. member for Pictou, it has now been changed by constituting a court of appeal, consisting of the two judges of the court and the Gold Commissioner. We have not in any ordinance provided for an appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada. I fully recognize that there is a good deal to be said in favour of a further appeal. A doubt exists whether that could be given by ordinance, in all probability an Act of parliament would be required. That, of course, would not involve any difficulty if it were considered wise as a matter of policy to have such an appeal. The principal difficulty I had in my mind in connection with the question of an appeal arose from the consideration that in deciding appeal cases myself, I found the most serious difficulty in thoroughly understanding the references to the markings on the ground. Although there were in some eases three or four or half a dozen plans made by surveyors on the ground, and although I had for several years given special attention to the mining regulations, and bad discussed the conformation of the ground with surveyors and other people familiar with it, yet I had great difficulty in one or two cases in being certain that I understood, from references in the evidence and the decision of the Gold Commissioner, the conformation of the ground. Many cases that came before me practically turned upou some fact to understand which it was absolutely necessary that a judge should know the nature of the country, and something about the conformation of the ground. It is almost impossible to tell this from the words used by witnesses. For instance, as an illustration, I may mention that the question in one case was as to where the base of a hill was. Witnesses on one side said it was at a certain point, and they described the conformation of the ground- how quickly the ground rose at that point

and the growth of grass and timber there- and they got back to the question whether this rising ground had been there 100 years or 200 years. The evidence was of such a character that it was next to impossible to a person who had never seen the country to understand what the evidence meant. 1 felt, therefore, that for the present at least, it was very doubtful if it would add anything to the probability of a just decision of such cases to take them from a court composed of two judges who are necessarily brought into familiarity with the facts and circumstances, to judges who would be altogether new to the mining regulations and the questions of fact which they would have to decide. I am quite of my hon. friend's opinion, that if on consideration it would seem probable that a more accurate decision would follow from an appeal to a higher court, in some cases we ought to give an appeal, because the value of the property is very great; but, so far as I have been able to give the question any consideration up to the present time, I am inclined to the view that the judges of the appellant court down here would find a serious difficulty in disposing of these appeals. They certainly would have to give an enormous amount of time to the study of the conditions before they could feel that they were giving justice to the suitors.

Of course, where the question was simply one of fact, there would be no advantage in taking a case beyond the Supreme Court of British Columbia to the Supreme Court of Canada ; for the Supreme Court of Canada have laid down the rule that where two courts below have dealt with the question of fact in the same way, they will not interfere with the finding ; at least, I think that is the usual course pursued by that court. But, I have in mind one case which occurred in the province of Nova Scotia fifteen or sixteen years ago, in which the decision of the Supreme Court of Nova Scotia was reversed by the Privy Council with/ respect to the construction of the mining Act of that province, and on the result of that decision depended the ownership of half a million dollars worth of mining lands. In an important case of that kind, where a question of construction arose, it would seem to be right that there should be an appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada.
Consolidation of Dominion statutes, orders in council and proclamations having the force of law, notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act, $20,000.
In what stage of advancement is the consolidation of the statutes ?
There is absolutely nothing done.
Can the hon. gentleman give us any information as to when it is expected to have the statutes consolidated ?
The intention is, when this vote goes through, to have an order in counil passed immediately, for the purpose of appointing commissioners.
Can the hon. gentleman give any information as to when they are likely to get through with the work ?

The last revision was begun in 1881 and completed in 1887. We hope to do the work more expeditiously, because we intend to utilize the services of some of the permanent officials to help in the work of consolidation.
Is the hon. gentleman going to have it done by the job or by the year ?
We have not considered that point, but will be glad to consider any suggestions that my hon. friend may have to offer as to adopting one course or the other.
What is the significance of the expression * notwithstanding anything contained in the Civil Service Act ' here ?

We intend to take advantage of the services of some permanent officials. There is no reason why the Deputy Minister of Justice should not be employed in important work of this kind. Other officials also should be able to render valuable assistance.

While that may be well, it may lead to abuse. The officials are paid for their whole time, and if you propose to employ them outside of their regular duties and pay them extra, the minister is left free to employ his own friends and give them any amount he pleases.

The intention is to select the most competent men. I do not wish to commit myself to anything 'when I say that we may not confine ourselves to the Department of Justice, but may ask the services of others, for instance, the law clerks of the Senate and the House of Commons. It is not expected that these gentlemen should work without additional remuneration. In the last revision, the deputy minister was paid a gratuity of $5,000 in addition to his salary of $4,000. I am not saying now what the intentions of the government are, because I do not know, but I think it proper to have the words, ' notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act,' so that if it is desired to utilize the services of permanent officials, that may be done.
Permanent officials, of course, are not supposed to work

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: during all their waking hours. They must have a certain amount of leisure, and there is no reason that I can see why they should not do some work in connection with the revision of the statutes and receive some additional remuneration for their work.

I understand my hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax) to refer to the possible contingency of the officials in the Department of Justice being employed after hours, but he also indicated that they would be employed during their regular hours. Of course, they could not charge extra for work done during these hours. But, if some of them are employed by the Minister of Justice after hours, the insertion of these words would enable him to pay them for their services.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES (Hon. Sir Louis Davies).

speechtext: That is what I thought I was saying. Every one, except members of parliament, has certain leisure, and these officials might be employed during a part of that leisure, in doing work of this kind, and there is no reason that I can see why they should not expect remuneration for it.

I do not object to giving-reasonable remuneration. But what I pointed tout was the danger of abuse. The case mentioned by the Solicitor General is a case in point. It is supposed that $4,000 is a fair salary for the deputy minister. Yet we paid him $5,000 for his services besides, we make his salary equal to or above that of the premier. Will anybody say that that is not an abuse ? I do not care which government was responsible for it, such an action is not to be upheld. But this would give the minister power to pay some of his officers extra, whether the work is done during the regular working hours or during their spare time. Leaving the money in the hands of the department to use it as they see fit, will lead to pressure being brought to bear by these employees to get as much of it as possible, and I think that very often they get more than they are really entitled to.

As I understand it, the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) objects to leaving in the words ' notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act.' The Solicitor General said that no policy had been announced as to employing anybody. It may possibly be that the services of experts in the Justice Department may be required, and in order to make that possible, these words are put in.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: I am not objecting, because, of course, the Civil Service Act provides that civil servants cannot get more than the amount voted for.

That is what we supposed
the law to be, though the Supreme Court has held otherwise.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: That is what we regard as the law now. There ought to be some understanding that we are paying them fail-compensation for their working time and that we are not to pay them an exorbitant price for extra work that they do. I admit that they can be properly employed in this work and that they should get proper remuneration for what they do. But I do not think that we should give any man $4,000 salary and $5,000 extra for his services during the same year.

I hope the Minister of Marine and Fisheries does not minimize the statement made by the Solicitor General. That hon. gentleman said, and I agree with him, that he was going to employ officers in his department and some officers out of other departments. He did not bind himself to the statement that he would not go outside of the department. But the Minister of Marine and Fisheries simply says that it is possible that some men in the Department of Justice may be employed.

The hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Haggart) is in error. I made no statement at variance with that made by the Solicitor General. That hon. gentleman did not lay down a policy, but said that putting the vote in this form was to enable the government, if they thought fit, to employ officers of the Justice Department.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext:
I would suggest that the experience of the gentlemen in the Department of Justice renders them particularly capable of doing work of this kind, and it would be a great pity if their services were not utilized in that way.
Dominion Lands-Chargeable to Income-Protection of timber lands In Manitoba and the North-west Territories and tree culture in the North-west Territories, $15,000.
This is a new item, is it not ?
There was a vote of $10,000 last year.
speakername: The MINISTER OF THE INTERIOR (Hon. Clifford Sifton).

speechtext:
I understand that the department is going to appoint a commissioner for Manitoba and one for the North-west Territories, and, when persons want to plant tree-breaks, they may write to the commissioner, and the commissioner will go or send some person to view the place and tell the kind of trees that will grow best in that soil, and will also make a rough sketch to be sent to headquarters, where a working plan will be prepared for the planting of the trees. The commissioner or his assistants will have the oversight of the planting of the trees and will visit them from time to time to see that they are properly cared for.

If that is to be done in that vast country, you will need to have a whole host of officials to carry out the law. It does seem to me that it is altogether unnecessary. You might as well undertake to direct and superintend any other part of the work of the farm as to take control of this tree-planting. We had the commissioner (Mr. Stewart) before the Committee on Agriculture, and he explained his plan. He went on to make these statements to us, and I would like to have from the minister a statement of what he intends to do with reference to these matters.

I have for a number of years believed that one of the most important needs in Manitoba and the North-west Territories was a plan that would prevent the destruction of timber lands by fire, and coupled with that some means of educating the farmers in an intelligent system of tree planting. A portion of this vote is for the purpose of providing for the protection of forests upon Dominion lands from fire, and that is a large share of the work which is done under the direction of this branch of the department. Another jiortion of the work is that which has been described by my hon. friend who has just taken his seat, as a means of bringing about an intelligent system of tree planting. I am confident that the committee will not begrudge this sum if they believe it can be used effectively for those two purposes. We do not suggest that there should be a system which would extend its ramifications all over the territories, under which we would meet every demand that might be made in this direction for a number of years to come. All we intend to do is to get the work started, feeling confident that if it is fairly and Intelligently started, the people themselves will take up and carry it along. It is in a small way much like what the Minister of Agriculture under this government and the Minister of Agriculture under the late government have done in the way of encouraging the dairy industry in the west where, on account of the special circumstances, that industry could not have been successfully started without government assistance. The primary object of this branch of the department was to provide protection for forests upon Dominion lands, with regard to which there has been a great and deplorable loss by fire in former years: and secondly, to institute, if possible, and in an educative way, a system by which the farmers may know the best kind of trees to plant and how to take care of them. If the experiment is successful, and the farmers can be encouraged to go extensively into tree planting, the result will be worth to the country much more than this small sum of money. I may say that I know of my own personal knowledge that efforts have been made for some years past Mr. WILSON.
to inaugurate a system of tree planting. I know of individuals who have spent a great deal of money and labour, but to no purpose, in a great many cases, because their efforts were 111 directed. I have considerable hope that the result of the efforts that we are making wTill be to show them a more successful way, and that they will attain more substantial results.

How many years has the hon. gentleman been engaged in this scheme ?
The	MINISTER	OF	THE	INTERIOR.
We took an appropriation for a superintendent two years ago.
Mr.	WILSON.	I presume	in talking
about the superintendent, the hon. gentleman refers to Mr. Stewart ?
The	MINISTER	OF	THE	INTERIOR.
Yes.

Do you Intend to appoint two more, one for Manitoba and one for the North-west Territories ?
The	MINISTER	OF	THE	INTERIOR.
We intend to appoint two assistants. We have appointed one gentleman already, but. not for any particular portion of the country, his name is Norman M. Ross. He is a gentleman who has made a special study of forestry. He took his course at the Guelph Agricultural College, was engaged for some time at the experimental farm at Indian Head, was subsequently in the employ of the Ontario government in forestry work, and then he went to North Carolina for the purpose of studying forestry under Dr. Schenk, who is one of the greatest authorities upon forestry. Subsequently he went to Europe where he spent a short time. It is my intention, if possible, to procure two forestry experts from Germany or Belgium.

The hon. gentleman has given the House what may appear to him as a reasonable explanation of this vote, but I venture to say that no sane man in Canada will say they are good reasons. He puts this scheme on a par with encouraging the dairy industry, why, they are as utterly dissimilar as two eases could be. One is a general interest, the other is an individual interest. The hon. gentleman proposes to construct, with the public funds of Canada, wind breaks for each individual who may call upon him. I admit there is great difficulty in that country in getting trees to grow; but does the hon. gentleman mean to say that men there are so devoid of sense that they do not know as well how to plant a tree as Mr. Ross does ? Why, any country boy knows that. The record he has given Mr. Ross is an astounding one. He has made too good a case for Mr. Ross, he is too well trained. He comes here with an outfit for Mr. Ross that

is utterly worthless. I would like to know what training he gets in the agricultural college at Guelph for forestry. Then he has been to South Carolina, and he has been to Europe. I venture to think that if the whole truth were told, Mr. Ross is a gentleman the lion. Minister of the Interior wants to take care of. Now in regard to Mr. Stewart, he never had any important duties to perform. Mr. Stewart appeared before the Agriculture Committee last year, and I am bound to say that he did not make a very creditable showing. He could not tell where the timber was upon the Crown lands that ought to be protected. All he was able to say was that there were considerable belts along the railways in British Columbia, where there was valuable timber. Whether that is so or not, does not materially concern the Dominion of Canada. The timber was upon the railway lands, and therefore the railway companies were interested jointly, if not solely, in that matter. Now what timber was there in the Northwest Territories and in that whole country that Mr. Stewart was able to say was of such vast importance that you should have fire wardens there to protect it ? It would be utterly impossible to man that country with a sufficient number of men to protect valuable timber if it already existed there. But in the first place it does not exist, so far as we have information; and I say Mr. Stewart was appointed to a place that was a mere sinecure. First of all, Mr. Stewart was appointed, and then the department set about to find duties for him. Now the hon. gentleman proposes to give him two new assistants, he is going to Germany to get experts to do what the common sense of every man in the country would suggest. I tell the hon. gentleman that he has not shown a shadow of justification for spending one copper for performing a service that belongs to each individual instead of to the public of Canada. So far as I am concerned I am going to take the sense of the House, if there are enough gentlemen to demand a vote with me. Where is this going to end ? Is the hon. gentleman going to make this a general service, or make it a special service for a few of his friends ? It is just as the member for Lennox (Mr. Wilson) said a moment ago. When a man wants a wind-break about his place, what does he do ? He sends down to the department at Ottawa to make a working plan to put out a few trees. Did any one ever hear of anything more ridiculous than that. And then the inspector is sent there to see whether the trees are well put out
With a watering can.

With a watering can, my hon. friend (Mr. Cochrane) says. I have no doubt that will be quite as sensible as the other part of the scheme-and more successful, my hon. friend says. The hon. minister says that this is educational. Is he
going to educate the whole country by building a wind-break 1 Certainly not. The first thing that must be sought in that country is the class of tree that will grow there. I believe that this plan was suggested to the hon. gentleman by persons who are- anxious to fill positions. I think the hon. gentleman has been imposed upon.
I am going to give him credit for being sincere and honest enough to have believed in the proposal that has been made to him, but he is the victim of a fraud and a sham.

I am afraid I cannot accept unreservedly the statement of the hon. member for Both-well (Mr. Clancy), that this plan is a fraud and a sham, nor can I accept the reasons he has given as good reasons for his belief. In the first place, he says that we had to find a place for Mr. Stewart, and that having appointed him, we had to give him something to do. I want to tell the hon. gentleman that his assumption is entirely incorrect. I think I know more about the workings of that branch of my department, than the hon. gentleman does.
If the hon. gentleman does, he knows more about it than Mr. Stewart does.
There was no officer of the department to * give special attention to the question of protection against forest fires, which were a source of great embarrassment before that to the department.
Will the hon. gentleman state to the committee where the valuable timber is in the North-west Territories ?

I can give the hon. gentleman the information that we have a great deal of valuable timber. There is timber upon the Moose Mountain timber reserve, where the late government made a reserve, and where, I think, in doing so, they acted with the utmost wisdom. They expended money for the purpose of preserving that timber. Most of it is not timber of a character that is fit for building purposes. But, it is timber which supplies fuel for the population for many miles around, and it would be most disastrous if that timber were to be destroyed. In the Turtle Mountain district, and up in the northern portion of Manitoba, on the north slope of the Riding Mountains, and along the streams which flow north-westward, upon the lines of railway going through the Lake Dauphin country to Prince Albert, there are considerable belts of valuable timber. The same can be said practically of the country around Lake Winnipeg, and for many years the department has been reaping quite a considerable revenue from the timber which has been operated in the districts to which I have referred. In addition to that, upon

the mainland of the Canadian Pacific Kailway in British Columbia, there is a large amount of valuable timber.
The hon. gentleman knows that that is in the railway belt, and as for Manitoba, Mr. Stewart, X do not think, proposes to go there at all.

My hon. friend made a mistake when he was speaking before, and if he will refrain for a moment, I will explain it so that he will not make the same mistake again. The land in British Columbia, which is known as the railway belt, belongs to the Dominion government and is under our administration. A large amount of the timber comes under the administration of the department, and that is a place where a considerable amount of care is necessary for the purpose of protecting the timber from fire.
I would like to ask the hon. gentleman if that timber in the railway belt has not entered into the hands of private individuals ? Has it not been sold ?

The hon. gentleman asks a question which cannot be answered wholly by yes or no. By far the greater portion of the timbered land in the proportion of, I should say, fifty to one, is still in the hands of the government. There are scattered homesteads and settled tracts in that vast tract of land, but the land that has passed from the hands of the government, as far as the soil is concerned, is a mere trifle. A considerable portion of the land has been disposed of in so far as the timber is concerned, and is held upon the same terms as timber berths are always held when they are disposed of by the department. So that, the impression of the hon. gentleman that there is no large amount of timber to be protected in British Columbia, is a mistaken one. There is a vast amount of timber, and if the hon. gentleman looked into the matter and found that there were no steps being taken to protect the timber, he would be the first, and very properly so, to criticise the department for gross neglect of duty. The hon. gentleman says that giving some instructions in regard to tree planting is for the purpose of benefiting individuals. That is perfectly true. But, my hon. friend is too late in the day when he is objecting to expenditures of this class being made, because their special benefit is not distributed equally over the whole community. We have experimental farms established by the late government and continued by this government, and I know that they have done an enormous amount of good throughout the country. But, the results of the experiments are not certainly distributed equally throughout the whole community. The benefits which accrue are more largely derived by the people in the immediate neighbourhood of the farms than by the whole Mr. SIFTON.
community, but the information and knowledge which are acquired in the operations that take place upon these farms can be made available by the whole community, and so can the information which will accrue in the case of the operations which will be conducted in connection with the plan I have suggested in the committee. My hon. friend, and I do not blame him, because I know a great deal more about the inhabitants of the western country than he does, is quite mistaken in regard to the views the people there take of this matter. The meetings which have been held, and to which the farmers have come for the purpose of discussing this matter with the superintendent of forestry, have been attended by the most intelligent farmers in that country, who have taken a very active interest in the question, and -who have been enthusiastically loud in their praises of the department for taking up this plan. It is the most intelligent of the farmers who take an interest in it, because they feel that if it can be shown without too great an expense that the farmer can grow a considerable number of trees upon his farm, his success will be an object lesson to those around him, and the work will then go on itself. One of the main difficulties in regard to tree planting heretofore has been the getting of planting material of a satisfactory kind. In Manitoba and the North-west Territories, the farmers have attempted to plant what is known as the Dakota cottonwood, and it has been in some places a success. Some few other trees have also been tried, but there has been no systematic trial of other kind of trees, which might be available for fire-guards and wind-breaks on the ordinary prairie farm. I have no doubt that the hon. member for Bothwell is perfectly honest in his criticisms. I can assure him that there is no intention on my part of doing anything except to employ the most competent person to give this suggested plan a reasonable trial. I know from experience that in so far as we are expending this money for the purpose of protecting the forests, we are only doing that which the government has always done, and which it is urgently required we should devote a little more attention to. In so far as the question of tree planting is concerned, I am perfectly satisfied that we may fairly expect to see substantial results in a short time.

The hon. gentleman says that as an instance of the intelligence of the people in that county they have held meetings and that they were very enthusiastic over the plan. I quite agree with him that it is an evidence of the intelligence of the people that they can conceive that a work they ought to perform for themselves is being performed out of the public purse. I think there is no better evidence of their intelligence that they have the best

of it, and that they should be enthusiastic is not a thing to be wondered at. Let us come back to the protection of timber. Mr. Stewart stated that the principal part of the railway belt was in the hands of private persons who had licenses to cut, and that there was a system of protection in operation with regard to these limits long before this government came into power. It was not necessary to appoint an inspector to rove all over the country, because these lessees were willing to pay a portion of the cost of protecting the timber against fire. Mr. Stewart admitted that it would he impossible to utilize enough labour to protect the scattered timber except in a very general way. The country is very sparsely inhabited and the chances of fire are very remote indeed.
As to the tree planting, I believe that an expenditure of money for the purpose of discovering what kind of trees would grow in that country might be justified, but for the minister to propose that plans of windbreaks will be sent to Ottawa and all that kind of thing, simply means that he is seeking some excuse to pay out money for unnecessary services. Our country is fast losing its timber. It is marvellous how the province of Ontario has been denuded, and although tree planting and re-foresting is a live question there, no one would propose to take up public funds for that purpose. If the minister would devote his attention to try and find what trees will grow in the North-west. I would be prepared to justify an expenditure of money for that, but it is absurd for him to propose to appoint men to plant trees when he does not know whether these trees will grow or not. The minister tells me that he knows that country and the people better than I do. That may be, but there is a common-sense view of this question which is apparent to every sensible man, and the proposal of the minister is not a common-sense one. What the minister proposes is practically to devote public money to; construct wind-breaks for private individuals. I hope he will reconsider that proposal and proceed upon intelligent principles.

My hon. friend (Mr. Clancy) seems to take particular objection to that suggestion which provides for a plan of wind-breaks being sent to Ottawa. I may say that when I looked into the matter myself I thought it would be too cumbersome, but that is a mere detail and not a necessary feature of the scheme at all. I can tell the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) that there have been experiments carried on at the Experimental Farm with regard to the class' of trees that would grow in the North-west Territories. To hand the materia! to the average prairie farmer would he simply waste. I cast no reflection on my constituents or on my friends in the North-west as regards their

industry or their capacity as farmers, but as a rule they have no experience in treeplanting. The great majority of them ^.re young men who have not heretofore made a success of their efforts in that direction, and it is because of this fact that the most intelligent farmers of the country have taken a great interest in this question, and have cordially approved of the proposal of the government. The main object is to furnish farmers with plant material, who are willing to take advantage of this proposition, and then we intend to see that the material is made proper use of so that we may have a few examples of success in the cultivation of trees, which in a short time will lead to general good results. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) is unduly pessimistic on the question of forestry, and he is not taking wise ground when he says that the public funds should not he used for this purpose. In some of the European countries public funds have been used in this way with marvellously beneficial results, and in a comparatively short space of time the whole face of one or two European countries has been changed by scientific forestry- If my hon. friend visits us in the North-west in a few years I am in hopes that I will be able to show him that the result of this expenditure has been beneficial.

The position taken by the minister now, is entirely at variance with that taken by Mr. Stewart before the committee. Mr. Stewart laid great stress upon the men who will have charge of the construction of the wind-breaks in that country, and he told us they should be men who had lived there for years, and who are well acquainted with the climate and the kind of trees. that would grow in the different districts. He said that if any person applied, a man would he sent out to show him how to plant trees, and to tell him the kind of trees that would be adapted to the nature of the soil. The minister leaves the impression on the committee that this is only a start, as it were, while Mr. Stewart in his evidence laid it down that they would appoint one commissioner in the North-west and one in Manitoba, that these would be sufficient for the present, but that they would need to have assistants in the near future. If, on application to one of these commissioners, he is obliged to send out a man to each farmer to give instruction as to how to construct a windbreak, any one can understand that we would need to have a large number of officials. That is what I object to. I believe that the information gathered from the experimental farms, and the natural common-sense knowledge that a man who has lived in that country for a number of years should acquire, ought to be sufficient, without having to send out a government official to specially instruct him. Besides that, the

minister says that Mr. Ross has been down in North or South Carolina to study the tree business, and now he is going to Germany ; which is totally at variance with the statements made by Mr. Stewart to the committee. He laid great stress on the importance of gaining information from actual experience derived from living in the country. I hope the minister has no idea of appointing a whole army of officials to teach the farmers in that country how to plant trees on the prairies.

This is a matter of so much importance to Manitoba and the Northwest Territories that instead of $15,000 being voted for this purpose, I think the sum should be much larger. The hon. gentleman who has just spoken should remember that whereas the older provinces possess their timber and public lands, the timber and public lands in Manitoba and the Territories belongs to the Dominion, The province of Ontario has spent a large amount of money not only in preserving its timber, but in reforesting.
Not one cent.
The province of Ontario has spent a large amount of money for this purpose ; I heard of it being discussed the other day in the local House. How many forest rangers are there in Ontario to-day?
An army of them.

Yes, and if they had been appointed years ago, the state of affairs mentioned by the hon. member for Russell (Mr. Edwards) the other day, that the province was almost denuded of timber, would not now exist. If the hon. gentlemen who sat in this House in 1882 and 1883 had taken the precautions to protect the timber about the Pembina Mountains, the farmers of that district would not be in the position they are in to-day, of having to haul coal from Roche Percee or Estevan, and pay $4.75 a ton for it. The amount of money received by the Dominion for stump-age on ties, saw-logs, for cord-wood, and things of that sort must be very large indeed-more than sufficient to pay the $15,000 mentioned here. The county which I have the honour to represent has, I believe, the largest quantities of timber of any county in the province. There are large quantities of spruce west of Lake Winnipeg, and north of the line of the Canadian Pacific Railway from East Selkirk to the eastern boundary of the province, and it is of the utmost importance that that timber should be protected. In fact, the city of Winnipeg derives its chief timber supply from that region. In the neighbourhood of the Riding Mountains, the Porcupine Hills, and Duck Hills, there are large quantities of timber, and if some precautions are not taken that timber will be destroyed, as the settlers going in set fire to the scrub for the purpose of clearing their land. If we had fire-Mr. WILSON.
breaks sixty-six or ninety-nine feet wide all around these mountains, liept ploughed and harrowed, so that the weeds would be kept down, and if fire did occur, the timber would be protected. With regard to tree-planting, that is a subject I know something about. In the city of Winnipeg eighteen or twenty years ago the people found great difficulty in getting trees to grow. Many men spent hundreds of dollars in the attempt. We tried to start parks in the city, but we did not succeed ; very few understood the nature of the soil and the most suitable trees. But a few years ago we appointed a park commissioner and to-day the city of Winnipeg has as fine parks as the city of Ottawa. At first the tree-planting was not a success ; but to-day we have fifteen or twenty miles of streets as well planted with trees as any streets in the city of Ottawa. That was not done until we had appointed a man who thoroughly understood the subject. We have fifteen or twenty parks in the city, some two acres in extent and others very large.
Was it Mr. Ross who made that discovery.

No, Mr. D. D. England, a gentleman from the old country, who was a gardener there, and who studied the question in this country. I have no knowledge at all of Mr. Ross, the gentleman spoken of ; but I submit that it is of the utmost importance to Manitoba and the North-west-Territories that this sum, and even a much larger sum, should be spent in the protection of timber and the encouragement of treeplanting.
Will the hon. gentleman say what kind of tree was successful In Winnipeg ?

Those planted on Broadway are elms. The first trees planted were the Red river maple, which in appearance is between the ash and the soft maple ; but fit was not a success. Where the soil is deep and heavy we have taken sand from Point Douglas and mixed it with the black soil, and where this was done not over 12 per cent of the trees on Broadway failed. It will take some time to study this question, and I think the minister might have gone even further than he has. I submit that the farmers themselves might do something in the way of tree-planting under proper instructions. The country along the line of the Canadian Pacific Railway west from Moosejaw, is all barren of trees except the Moose Mountain, and the timber there is all small timber. When a man wants trees planted, the homestead entry, instead of being $10, might be increased to $20 or $25. Many men would gladly pay from $50 to $100 for a homestead with trees planted on it. This matter is one of great importance, and in view of the fact that the province of Manitoba and the Territories are

not the possessors of their own timber, it becomes the duty of this government to protect what they need as much as light and air, that is, timber for fuel.
Might I ask the hon. gentleman if he thinks it necessary to send a special man to every farmer to give him instructions how to plant a wind-break ?
I do not think that necessary at all ; but if an instructor went and explained to two or three farmers in a municipality, how it should be done, the balance would learn from them.

I think the hon. gentleman who has just spoken has done great service. He has completely answered the Minister of the Interior. He has candidly told the House that there is no difficulty in growing certain kinds of trees, for it has been done in the city of Winnipeg. All you have to do is to plant elms, and you will have plenty of growth in the country.
The hon. gentleman misunderstands me. What will suit the city of Winnipeg may not suit the Pembina Mountains, where the soil is entirely different.

The hon. gentleman has not helped his case. If he had said that the trees that grew in Winnipeg would not grow elsewhere, he might have a case ; but his argument was the opposite of that. After the speech the hon. gentleman has made, the Minister of the Interior is without any excuse. All he need do is to furnish the kind of tree plants suitable to a locality, and let the people plant the trees for themselves. The hon, gentleman scouts the idea of the people being able to do this. It is a slander on the intelligence of these people, many of whom come from the older provinces, to say that they know nothing about tree-planting. I dare say the Minister of the Interior has brought a class of people to the country, who live by camp fires, and who might require assistance in tree-planting, as well as assistance to keep body and soul together in many cases. But I venture the statement that three-fourths of the people, in fact, every man in Manitoba and the Territories who is worth having there, knows how to plant a tree, because he is guided by common sense, and has had experience in the older provinces, and is acquainted with a great many of the varieties of timber that obtain in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec. All these people would require would be to be furnished with the kind of tree plants suitable to their locality. It may be perfectly true that a class of timber that will grow in Winnipeg would not grow elsewhere ; but the business of the government could not reasonably go beyond assisting and furnishing tree plants that are suitable to a locality. This is a service that belongs to individuals and should not be paid for out of the public
purse. I still believe that the hon. gentleman has completely answered the Minister of the Interior, and I would ask the hon. gentleman to answer the hon. gentleman who has spoken on his own side.

I fancy the hon. gentleman from Bothwell (Mr. Clancy) has not travelled much in Manitoba and the North-west Territories. It is a very large country. As has just been remarked, though certain classes of trees may grow well in the city of Winnipeg, it does not follow that they will grow in every part of Manitoba and Territories. There are large parts of the Territories in which the people have not yet learned what trees grow to best advantage. As to protecting the timber, that ought to have been done years ago. I have been in the part of the country where I now live for the past twenty years, and I know that there have been immense quantities of timber destroyed by fire. And this occurs not merely where there is settlement, though the hon. member for Bothwell suggested that where there was no settlers there was no danger of fire.
I said it was remote.

A certain amount of this timber may belong to private parties, for I think about 15,000,000 acres of it was given away while hon. gentlemen opposite occupied the Treasury benches. Still, I can inform the hon. gentleman that there is a great deal of good timber belonging to the people of this country. The people in the older provinces own the timber lands within the limits of those provinces; but, the forest lands of the North-west are owned by the people of the Dominion as a whole. And, it is time that something was done to protect the timber there. In my own experience, there is township after township -yes, hundreds of them-where heavy timber grew ten or fifteen years ago and where there is now nothing but blackened stumps.

That is an important statement, but it is a contradiction of the statement made by Mr. Stewart to the committee. If Mr. Stewart, an official of the government, has made a statement contrary to that of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Davis) who says he knows the facts, that fact is important.

I was not at the meeting of the committee, and so do not know what Mr. Stewart said. I am merely telling the hon. gentleman that I know places in the Northwest Territories where, a few years ago, there were large forests and now there is nothing but prairie with some blackened stumps. That forest was very valuable, and if it had been protected it would have been there yet. One case that I recall is along the line of the Canada Northern Railway. There were immense forests there. I was through them twenty years ago. Two or three years ago I had occasion to go out

to tlie same place, and found nothing but prairie with a few back sticks. Not only is that timber valuable in itself, but it is particularly valuable as bringing us immigration, because the presence of timber there is very important. Young timber is springing up in those places, and it grows very rapidly. Take the poplar of the North-west Territories and Manitoba, and it does not take more than ten years to grow trees that are fit for rails. There are many instances in the North-west Territories of forests being destroyed by fire.

I desire to ask the hon. gentleman a question for information. If this country reforests so readily as he states, is it not an easy thing to replant these wind-breaks for farmers without government assistance ?
_ Mr. DAVIS. The hon. gentleman is talking as though he supposed the North-west Territories to be the same in every part. I am speaking of places where there have been trees. But there are millions of acres where there are no trees, but where, I feel prefectly sure, trees can be grown. But the people do not know what kind of trees will grow best. If the hon. gentleman will visit the Indian Head farm, he will see what trees are being grown there. But the trees in use so far do not last. An insect attacks them and kills them. If we could find a tree that would grow and last, we could turn that prairie almost into a garden. Wind-breaks are of the utmost value and enable grain to be grown where otherwise it could not be grown.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Davis) mentioned that there are large forests there. What kind of trees are they chiefly ?
There is a class of white poplar, some of which grow very large. There is also spruce and what is known as the jack pine or cypress pine and others.
How large an area would these townships of which the hon. gentleman speaks-I do not suppose they are all in one block ?

I suppose they would cover five or six hundred miles. My own district,
I suppose the hon. gentleman knows, is seven hundred miles long. On the north side it was heavily timbered, but a great deal of that timber was destroyed by fires. There is young timber growing up and we feel that it should be protected, because it will make valuabe timber in a few years. Take, for instance, the country from Prince Albert to Green Lake, and there are miles and miles of valuable timber destroyed in the last few years by forest fires, that, with a proper system, might have been saved.
What would the hon. gentleman suggest as the best mode of protection ?

Where there is timber, men should be appointed as fire guardians. I suppose it would not be necessary to pay them very high wages. They should travel about and see that parties going into the woods carefully put out any fires they make, or if not, to prosecute such parties.

A prairie fire may start from any of a hundred different reasons. When it gets a start, is there any protection you can place around the forest in this way to protect the forest ? I am asking for information.

My hon. friend (Mr. McCreary) pointed out how, by ploughing and keeping the weeds from growing up you can make a perfect protection. At the same time, we should have fire guardians whose business it is at certain seasons-I suppose it would not be necessary to pay them all the year round-say, after the harvest when the grass commences to get dry, to be out all the time to see to it that fires are put out.
Would it be possible to make a system of fire guards without a great deal of expense ?
Yes. It is not expensive. Two or three scrapes of a plough, then leave ten or twelve feet, then two or three more scrapes of the plough, and burn the grass between-that will make a protection.
But would that be of use in the case of a forest fire ?

I was referring to little groves such as I supposed my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) was speaking of. For large tracts of valuable timber, we should have fire guardians with duties as I have suggested.

Frequently a prairie fire can be seen twenty miles off. If a prairie fire was observed that endangered timber, I take it, it would be the duty of fire guardians to go out and burn a piece one or two hundred yards wide, so that the fire could not cross and get at the timber. He would take men with him with wet bags to prevent the fire he made from spreading beyond the desired limit.
Does the hon. gentleman think that that is possible as a practical means of protection, in such a wide area ?

I may mention that on one occasion when I was at a station forty-six miles south of Edmonton, a mounted policeman named Kitchen-there is only one stationed there-looked across the prairie and saw something and said to another party : Is not that smoke ? He went and got his glass, and said it was smoke, and within three minutes that man was on his horse, with his blankets and saddle, and started off for that fire. I afterwards inquired how he got along, and

found that although the fire was nearly seven miles away, he went there and got the neighbours out and they crushed it. A great portion of the duty of the mounted police is in stopping fires.

Does the minister intend to take the suggestion of the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. McCreary) and make experiments in certain localities, or does he intend to send a man to every person that applies to him for wind breaks ?

It appears that it is a very difficult matter to prevent fires in the Northwest. I understood the aim of this vote was to give instructions to farmers how to plant trees for their own protection. If that is the case, I do not see why an exception should he made in favour of the farmers of the North-west. There is quite as much need of forestry work in the other provinces. There is no money spent in this direction in the province of Quebec, and I think we have as good a claim as the North-west.

There is a vast difference between Manitoba and the North-western territories and the older provinces. That is a prairie country, and it is to the common interest of the whole Dominion that tree planting should be encouraged there. This is not a sectional question at all. That country has got past the experimental stage, and I think the $15,000 spent in instructing the people to plant trees on the prairie will be spent in the right direction, for it will make the country more valuable and more attractive to settlers. My hon. friend has mentioned the usefulness of the mounted police in putting out fires. But there are many portions of the North-west where there are no mounted police and which require to be protected.

I did not speak from a sectional standpoint, but it seemed to me to be an exceptional vote. Is it not possible that in the North-west, at the present stage of advancement, that people know what trees they ought to plant ? If they know what kind of trees to plant, why should we spend money to promote forestry in that section of the country more than in any other ?
I have said that there was a certain class of trees that the people thought was the proper kind for that country some years ago, but which turned out to be a failure.
Does the hon. gentleman not think it would be better to send them the trees and let the people plant them themselves ?
You would require to consider the climate, the soil and all that sort of thing. You might get trees from the experimental farm, and not one in a hundred of them would grow.

I remember years ago the director of the experimental farm told us they were carrying on experiments at Brandon, and at the experimental farms at Indian Head, and at Agassiz, to ascertain what kind of trees were best suitable for that country, and that they had acquired a great deal of useful information in that respect. Now whatever work was done then, the people could take advantage of in the several localities. He spoke also of the cultivation of different kinds of trees in different localities. All that was in the proper direction. But this vote, if it is to be of any use, it seems to me, should be much larger than it is. The object is the protection of timber lands in Manitoba and the Territories, and tree culture of the Northwest Territories. Now' from the information the member for Selkirk has given us, it seems it would require a whole army of fire rangers to keep down these fires. We know that once the fire is started on the prairie, especially if there is any wind, it extends very rapidly. I have seen a belt of fire extending fifteen, twenty or thirty miles in the night. What an immense number of men it would require to put out these fires. Many years ago when Prof. Macoun was before the Agriculture Committee he was asked the question why that country was a prairie country, and not covered with trees. He said it was because extensive fires ran over it almost every year, started by Indians, or half-breeds, or travellers. He was asked if it was possible to prevent these fires from starting, and he answered that it could only be done by employing an army of men. I can imagine that $15,000 will not go far in that direction. But the hon. member for Selkirk reminds us that we have a lot of men in Ontario engaged as fire rangers and timber inspectors, looking after the replanting of forests. I am not aware that there is any replanting going on in Ontario. I can tell him that these are a very valuable class of men to the Ontario government. One of the most important services they render to the government is in connection with the by-elections. They are always available then, always ready to serve their masters from time to time. The fire rangers, timber inspectors and that class of men are very plentiful. Mr. D. F. MacDonald, who has been well known for the last twenty-five years in Ontario, was so actively interested in the preservation of the forests that whenever there was an election he always came to the front. When there was an election in Algoma he went out and corralled the Indians and squaws in one house, he took the Indians out to vote for the government candidate, then took them back into the house, made them undress, and made the squaws put on the pants and coats and go and vote. And so he kept it up all day, and then boasted afterwards that he had put between sixty and seventy-five votes in for his candidate and got him elected. No
2G87

doubt be was a very valuable man, and no doubt the present government, especially the Minister of the Interior, very much desires a class of officers of that character under his control. They would be very valuable in carrying on elections. Cap Sullivan is another. I might mention a number of them, because I have been acquainted with their work. They are always available, always on hand whenever there is an election going on. They are more ardent in the discharge of their duties at that time than during any other time of the year. I notice that the present government are closely following the course pursued by their friends in Ontario, that is, they are constantly manufacturing offices for their friends and filling them. They are getting any army of men pensioned on the country, and it requires a large share of the consolidated revenue to pay these pensioners. The government appear anxious to multiply offices in which they can put their friends. Every man who is a defeated candidate, who has been an active election agent, they try to reward by giving him an office, and as offices are becoming scarce they are trying to create new. ones. Now it would be possible effectually to control these fires, but I do not believe that can be done without a large army of men. The hon. member for Selkirk will admit that they have men already engaged in the North-west, some paid by salary and some by commission. The expenditure is creeping up all the time, but the results do not compare with the expenditure. I think the expenditure of money is out of all proportion to the benefit that accrues from it. I would be very far from discouraging a reasonable effort to ascertain what trees would be suitable for planting in that country. But, I think that the men who have lived in that country for years ought to know more about that than men coming from other countries that have entirely dissimilar conditions. I do not think that the appointment of a large army of men will ever be for the benefit of the country or even for the benefit of the men who are appointed. It will create a great army of pensioners in that country.

Surely the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) does not believe that a great army of pensioners is going to be appointed with a vote of $15,000. He says this grant is too small, and I think it is too small.
I know the picture the hon. gentleman has drawn of the officials in Ontario, but he must not think that the people of the Northwest Territories are exactly the same as he represents them. The people of the Northwest Territories, from a political standpoint, do not need forest rangers to be placed there at the present time. We have all the majorities we want without the appointment of forest rangers or anything of that kind. In reference to the value of the men who are appointed for the express purpose of put-

ting this- plan into force, the hon. gentleman says that if a prairie fire started these men cannot do anything to stamp it out. If you have a forest ranger and he sees smoke five or six miles away, if he starts off when he sees the smoke, he can put the fire out, and in this way he would save probably more than it would cost to pay his salary for ten years. I do not think we require a vast army of politicians for that purpose, and a vast army could not be appointed with a vote of $15,000. I think the vote is too small. The hon. gentleman says that the farmers of the west are sufficiently intelligent to take this work upon themselves, but I would remind him that the men who have been in that country for years most heartily approve of this proposal of the hon. minister. They think it is a step in the right direction.

I have never yet seen any one who would refuse to accept an expenditure of money in his own locality. What I was drawing attention to was the description given by the hon. member for Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis), and the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. McCreary), of the vastness of the country in which this work is to be done. I say that to make it effective it would require a large army, and this sum would not be anything like equivalent to the necessities, if you are to do effective work. This is only the commencement of it, and it will be enlarged very rapidly in the future, just as the need occurs for places for disappointed politicians. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Davis) says that the scheme would be most valuable for putting out prairie fires, and that a ranger would be able to put out a fire if he saw it fifteen or twenty miles away. Does he imagine that during the time he would be travelling fifteen or twenty miles the fire would remain in the same locality ? A prairie fire will sometimes travel as fast as a horse.
The hon. gentleman is alluding to prairie fires ; there are bush fires that could be put out.

They all commence on the same principle as prairie fires. They lead from the prairie to the bush. I remember very distinctly seeing a prairie fire. We saw it in the evening, and the next morning, when I saw it, it appeared to me to be twenty miles off, but in half an hour we had reached the edge of it, because it had travelled very much faster towards us than we had travelled towards it. People in that country are obliged very often to start a fire whei'e they are to burn the prairie around them, and thus save themselves. Farmers there have had experience when whole districts of the country have been burned over. Notwithstanding the fact that the country is thickly settled, and that they get their teams out and

plough their fields for fire breaks, the fires jump over the ridges, and their crops and barns are burned. This shows how helpless a man would be in the ease of a fire spreading like that. When a neighbourhood that is moderately thickly settled cannot stop a fire or keep it under control in a locality, it shows that a very large army of men would be required to do anything like effective work in a country like that.

I am more than astonished that there is an intelligent man standing on the floor of this House and saying for one moment that any ordinary farmer thoroughly understands the planting of trees. Now, I would like to see the farmer who knows how to plant trees. There is as large an amount of experience required to plant trees properly as there is in doing any other work, but, after you have learned how to plant out trees, you want to know the trees to plant. I defy any man who has not had a good deal of experience to go into the forest, pick out trees, to plant them on the roadside and have them on the roadside and have them live. That is a thing you do not understand, and it is a thing that you should find out. What we want is to thoroughly understand the kind of trees that are suitable, and then we want to instruct the farmers how to plant them. Let a man under ordinary circumstances go into the woods and take out evergreen trees, and see what kind of work he will make of it. He simply cannot do it. Take some kinds of evergreen trees, and if the roots are planted on a dry or windy day no man can make them live. There is so much resinous matter in the roots of these trees, that unless they are planted on a wet day you cannot make a success of them at all. In reference to the fire rangers, we have Are rangers in my riding of South Renfrew. We have men that we hire to go and put out the fires, and they put them out successfully. They have voted against me as well as for me, and they are not Indians or squaws clothed in men's pants. They are white men, they are intelligent, and they know how to put out fire. Some of them belong to the Conservative ranks. It does not make any difference whether a man is a Conservative or a Reformer. If he knows how to put out fires, that is the kind of a man we want. The Ontario government assists in that work, they pay these men because they know how the work of extinguishing fires can be done. I think that the matter of $15,000 to assist men to plant trees in the North-west Territories is too small, and it is a wonder to me that the department did not make it $50,000 instead of $15,000.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Wright) pretends to say that it requires an expert knowledge to do this work, and that no farmer understands it. What expert knowledge had Mr. Stewart in that line, who is placed over the whole body of them ?
He was only an ordinary surveyor, taken off the farm, and ordinary enough at that. That is all the expert knowledge he has. and yet he is sent out to instruct the farmers.
I was not talking about the farmers ; I was talking about planting trees.

I should judge that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Wright) has no farmers in his locality. I am sure that the farmers in his county must be gratified at the certificate of character that the hon. gentleman has given them this evening. He has stamped them with the indelible stamp of stupidity. They know nothing. I did not know that the farmers were any more ordinary than the merchants. I thought they were usually a class of people who were equal in intelligence to any other class. I think their business in life has led them more particularly to the planting of trees than has that of the merchant class. I do not know whether the hon. gentleman is an expert tree planter himself or not ; he did not say so, but he has hinted at it. I repudiate the slander placed upon the farmers of this country, that they do not know how to plant trees. There are people who say that the farmers do not know enough to come in out of the rain. But, I tell the hon. gentleman that if there is any class of the community that knows anything about tree planting it is the farmers. There is scarcely a farmer who has not had the ambition, the thrift and the good taste to put trees about his place, notwithstanding that he has a forest surrounding it.
How many does he plant for one that grows ?

The farmers put out their trees in the fall. I tell the hon. gentleman who takes exception to that that he does not know anything about tree planting. He should go to the persons who put out trees regularly every fall. Trees are put out in the fall for the simple reason that no growth takes place then. If the earth stays around the roots of the trees and it retains its mois-, ture, the chances are ninety-nine to one that the trees will grow. The hon. gentleman said he had nothing to say about Mr. Stewart, and to that extent he repudiated Mr. Stewart's qualifications. I know Mr. Stewart from a hoy. He is a gentleman of great respectability ; he belongs to a good family. There is nothing to be said against Mr. Stewart personally only what is very much to his credit, and it would be a cowardly thing to say anything against Mr. Stewart in a place where he could not defend himself. But Mr. Stewart was a provincial land surveyor, and while he is a gentleman of great respectability, I do not suppose he ever planted half a dozen trees in his life, if he ever planted one. He left his home on the farm when he was a small boy and



therefore had not any experience in that direction. Mr. Stewart is possessed of common sense like other people, but he has no more common sense or experience than other people in tree planting. Surely, farmers who are brought up on the farm, although their experience in tree planting be limited, ought at least have as much knowledge as other individuals in this direction.

I do not for a moment think that It is an accusation against any farmer to say that he does not understand the planting of trees, any more than it would be to say that he cannot make a wagon wheel, although he uses wagons every day in the year. It is ridiculous for the hon. member (Mr. Clancy) to say that a man can plant trees in this section of the country in the fall, and expect them to grow. I have had some experience in this matter and I can tell the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) that any man who would undertake to plant trees in the fall and make a success of the business, would deserve a leather medal from the hon. gentleman. There is just as much skill required in planting trees as there is in growing a good crop of wheat, and it is not every man who knows anything about that. Some of the settlers in the North-west come from all parts of the world. They often come from large cities, where they perhaps never as much as even saw a tree, and you might as well expect the wives of these men to make good butter as to expect that the men themselves can successfully plant trees. That branch of farming requires more skill than a man who has never had anything to do with it thinks. A great many people think that all they have to do is to dig a hole and put a tree in it, and stamp the earth around it, and that the tree will grow. That is not the case by any means. It wants a good deal of experience to make a successful tree planter, and a man. should almost serve his apprenticeship to it. You want to know what kind of tree you are going to plant, and whether or not it will thrive in that particular soil, and in that locality. Many a tree that will grow in the woods will not grow in the open. As to Mr. Stewart, I have no doubt that he is a good and amiable man, and if lie comes from the same section of the country as the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy), why should he not be amiable and intelligent, and know a good deal about planting trees, the .same as the hon. gentleman himself does.

Would the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) inform us why the experimental farms were started. The Conservative government get credit for starting the experimental farms, and it certainly is no reflection upon the farmers of Canada that these experimental farms were inaugurated. Neither is it a reflection on the farmers that this government has undertaken to find out Mr. CLANCY.
what kind of trees would be suitable for certain portions of the country.

I can tell the hon. gentleman (Mr. Davis) the object of starting the experimental farms. One object of the experimental farm in the North-west was to do the very work which the minister now proposes to put his hand in the public purse for. Why not leave that business to the experimental farm. It is no reflection on the farmers of Canada that experimental farms were started, but I can tell the hon. gentleman that the the young men who have studied at the experimental farms have never been able to carry their teaching into practical effect when they went to work on their own farms.
I defy any one to point to half a dozen men who attended the Ontario Agricultural College who have followed out the methods they were taught there when they cultivated their own farms. In that respect it has been a dismal failure. The conditions of the land in different localities vary so much that it is impossible to lay down any general scientific principle which can govern. There are [DOT] two or three principles which the common sense farmer has at his command which are applicable all over, and the best farmers in the country are those who mastered these principles without ever seeing an agricultural college. I admit the value of the agricultural college for the purpose of testing seeds and so on, but for the purpose of training men to farm, it has been a dismal failure in the greatest province of the whole Dominion, notwithstanding that there have been hundreds of thousands of dollars expended on it. I repeat that the best farmers we have in Canada are not the young men. who went to the Agricultural College, but they are the men who mastered the conditions of their own farms and who by their industry and sturdy common sense were able to make their way without knowing anything of any real or affected science about farming.
How many forest rangers has the minister in his employ in the province of Manitoba, and what are their duties ?

I think I gave the hon. gentleman (Mr. Roche, Marquette) the answer to that on a former occasion. The homestead inspectors are required to act as forest rangers whenever they are instructed by the Crown timber agent. The head timber inspector at Winnipeg is authorized to instruct the homestead inspectors in their duties as forest rangers. In addition to the homestead inspectors, there is a forest ranger, Mr. Trudel, having his headquarters at Regina ; one at Edmonton and one at Turtle Mountain. The plan which it is proposed to work out under this vote is that the homestead inspectors or the forest rangers, as the case may be, will

be instructed at a particular season of the year to employ such men as they think necessary for thirty or forty days temporarily. These men have printed instructions in the form of a book, and they have printed forms containing the clauses of the law which provide penalties for starting fires and that sort of thing, and they post these notices and warn the people of the district. Last year we did not require to employ any, because just at the dangerous season of the year, which lasts about six weeks, very heavy rains came on and it was not necessary to make appointments, so that the money voted for that purpose was saved. Under ordinary circumstances a very great deal of work can be done for three or four thousand dollars, at $3 a day, for the men and the conveyance, and when these men are only employed temporarily. The intention in regard to the whole plan is that we have a superintendent and an assistant superintendent, who has given special attention to forestry, and we expect to employ in the west a couple of supervisors who are thoroughly familiar with, and will be specialists in that class of work. I shall not discuss at length the points raised by my hon. friend (Mr. Clancy), because I do not think that I need take seriously a great many things that he said. Most of his protests were directed against work which has been done by the Department of the Interior since it was instituted, namely, the taking of reasonable precautions against the destruction of timber, and that work must always be done by any department of government having timber lands under its charge. The argument of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) would go against doing anything at all. So far as this particular vote is concerned, it is simply an enlargement to the extent of two or three thousand dollars of a vote which has heretofore been always paid out of the Dominion lands appropriation.

Does the minister intend to utilize the present forest rangers for this work. He has only told us of three forest rangers who are homestead inspectors in the Territories. He has told us that he has some forest rangers in Manitoba who are not homestead inspectors.

There is no permanent officer a member of the local legislature.
Is not Mr. Jerome in the employ of the government as forest ranger ?

I am told that the gentleman to whom my hon. friend refers was formerly a member of the civil service, but he resigned his position when he became a candidate for the local legislature. He has been employed temporarily, but he is not a permanent officer of the department.
What salary does he get now, and what did he get before ?
He does not get any salary now.
What amount of money per annum does he draw from the public treasury 1
