I understand the minister to say that out of this vote of $15,000 there are employed for about forty days every year the several inspectors of homesteads on account of the danger of fire ?

No. What I meant to say was that the homestead inspectors are salaried officers paid out of another vote; but they are employed by the Crown timber agent for the purpose of protecting the forests from fire when so instructed. Then it is intended to employ some farmers in the neighbourhood for a short time.
Are both of these parties to be paid out of this $15,000 ? The minister mentioned that a permanent instructor with two assistants would be employed. Do their salaries come out of the $15,000 vote ?

Yes. I will give the hon. gentleman the figures : The superintendent, $2,500; the assistant superintendent, $1,000 ; two supervisors, $1,500 ; traveling expenses for all the officers of the department, $2,000 ; printing notices and directions such as I have mentioned, $1,500 ; plant material, $1,500 ; building fire guards, $1,000 ; and the payment of men who may be employed temporarily in the fall, $4,000.
These persons specially employed would not be inspectors of homesteads ?
No, the homestead inspectors are not paid out of this vote at all.
Those would be special employees for six weeks ?
Yes, special employees.

I understand that the mounted police, the homestead inspectors and the timber inspectors, all join in protecting the timber in that country from fire, and also that they have a right to employ other persons for a short period for the same purpose, and that they are paid out of another vote. Now, the hon. gentleman is asking $15,000 to supplement that service.

My hon. friend is not taking into account the size of the district of the homestead inspector. I venture to say it is on the average from 200 to 400 miles, certainly from 200 to 300 miles. There are only four special timber inspectors engaged for a distance of 1,200 or 1,400 miles ; and they are employed in certain localities where their time is almost wholly taken up. The homestead inspectors' time is fully taken up. They simply act for a short time, because we do not want to go to the expense of employing special men when we have these men who are familiar with the country and the people. The object is to utilize for this work the staff we have.

Quite so ; but these gentlemen are covering the territory in that limit, and they are also in a position to call out farmers or others who must obey them, and these farmers are reasonably paid for assisting to protect their own property. Therefore, the machinery may be put in motion entirely irrespective of the chief inspector or those under him. The hon. gentleman will not say that the service has become more efficient by appointing one or two inspectors for the whole country. I am unable to see that by employing this new service the hon. gentleman has greatly remedied the difficulties that existed before. Mr. Stewart went over that country for the purpose of learning the extent of the timber in it. and he was appointed in the session of 1897 for a service unheard of before, and now it has developed into tree planting, because outside of that he has nothing to do. The hon. gentleman's statement has made it pretty dear that only about 10 per cent of this $15,000 is to be devoted to tree planting, whereas 90 per cent of it practically goes into the pockets of his own officials.

The hon. gentleman is surely carrying his argument to an unfair length. I must say
that I think the hon. gentleman's argument absurd. I never said that this was altogether for the encouragement of tree planting. The vote states specifically that it is for two purposes; and I stated that it was for the two purposes of protecting the forests and tree planting. The superintendent of forestry has been in office for two years, and his salary has been voted by the House after discussion; and the animus displayed by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) and other hon. gentlemen at that time is enough to account for the unnecessary length of this discussion. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) understands that this work cannot be carried on without officers, and I venture to say that no hon. gentleman, will say that, for carrying out the plan outlined the officers are too many. I agree with my hon. friend from Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis) that the vote is a very modest one, considering the work that we are expected to do. We anticipate being able to show good results by carrying on systematic work on these lines for a few years. My hon. friend attempted to leave the impression with the House that this vote of $15,000 except $3,000 would go into the pockets of officials. Having heard the statements and the arguments, he ought not to have tried to leave that misleading impression with the House. The arguments of hon. gentlemen opposite have undergone an entire change during this discussion. At first they said we would require a complete army of men. That was repeated several times. And now the hon. gentleman gets up and says we have too many men. I think that the simple plan that I have explained to the committee a dozen times must commend itself to every man of common sense who has a knowledge of the circumstance as the only plan that can be carried out. We are making use of the ordinary officials of the department, the homestead inspectors, who are familiar with the country and who will take charge of the work. If it is necessary to hire men to protect the forests, these officers are authorized to hire them. Anybody familiar with the country will say that an enormous amount of work in the protection of forests can be done for $4,000. A reasonable explanation having been given and these hon. gentlemen having expressed their views, I do not know how they can justify taking up the time of the House with further discussion.

I am sure the committee will be obliged to the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Sifton) for his lecture. He says that the animus shown on the appointment of Mr. Stewart justified him in the position he takes. Objection was taken to the appointment of Mr. Stewart, not because it was Mr. Stewart, but because Mr. Stewart or any other person would be a useless official. The hon. gentleman has said that we have veered around during

this discussion. That is not the case. It was said that to give a service that would i cover that country would mean the employment of an army of men, but it was stated at the same time that there might he an efficient service made up, of the mounted police, timber agents and homesteads inspectors who are on the ground, assisted by the settlers whose services could be enlisted.
If the hon. gentleman thinks he defends himself by declaring that there was objection to the appointment of Mr. Stewart or anybody else on personal grounds, he is welcome to that opinion. Why, the minister had hardly warmed the seat he now occupies before he appointed Mr. Stewart. Nobody doubts the hon. gentleman's industry or ability in mastering the details of his department; but, knowing how little time he had, we may well doubt his knowledge at the time he appointed Mr. Stewart. I have nothing to say against Mr. Stewart except that he has been pensioned upon the service of this country for many years. He was employed by the province of Ontario, and when his work ceased there, he had to be taken care of, and the hon. minister took care of him. I have no doubt that the hon. gentleman (Mr. McCarthy) who is whispering to the Minister of the Interior now is telling him Mr. Stewart's history. Mr. Stewart was the Liberal candidate in North Simcoe against the uncle of the hon. gentleman who is coaching the Minister of the Interior. He was defeated there, and a place had to be found for him. And a place was found which was as worthless then as the one he occupies now is. He could never make it important

Mr. McCarthy. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) is making it very important.

My hon. friend (Mr. McCarthy) is the last one that should have anything to say on this subject. He did not welcome Mr. Stewart as a candidate in North Simcoe, and I am sure that lie is satisfied that Mr. Stewart should be appointed to office that he might be taken care of when he did not succeed in carrying a constituency. The Minister of the Interior says that hon. gentlemen on this side in criticising the appointment of Mr. Stewart are moved by personal animus. I appeal to the minister himself that that is not very high politics. He should be able to give better arguments than that. I do not propose to detain the committee with further discussion
Hear, hear.

I am sure that the hon. gentleman who says ' hear, hear,' would say exactly the same if thousands of new officials were being fastened upon the service of this country. But see what this multiplication of officials leads to. The country to be covered by this service is a
vast country. The hon. minister, in his supplementary estimates, is asking for more money for the outside service in connection with Dominion lands. I do not discuss that now, but I merely refer to the fact that this is not all the money that will be required. It only shows that when you multiply officials you are in the hands of these officials, you lose control of your expenditures and must increase them to serve these officials rather than to serve the interests of the country.,
That item being passed, we will take up No. 246.
But the hon. gentleman should take this up item by item. That is the custom.

But all the other items were passed, this one being held over in order to give the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) an opportunity to express his views.
Expenses of government in district of Keewatin, $2,190.

Of this sum, $600 goes towards the salary of the lieutenant-governor, $480 is for stenographer, and the balance of the money is taken up for the travelling expenses of the lieutenant-governor, who goes out about once a year, and some small expenses for printing and stationery.
Maintenance of lunatics from Keewatin, $2,000. The MINISTER OF THE INTERIOR. The district of Keewatin is a sort of noman's land, which, for administrative purposes, comes under the jurisdiction of the lieutenant-governor of Manitoba. The lunatics are brought down from that region to the asylum in Manitoba, and their maintenance is paid for by the Federal government to the provincial authorities. We-have generally taken a vote of $3,000 ; but we think this year $2,000 is likely to be sufficient.
For the relief of distressed Canadians in foreign countries other than the United States, $500.

This vote is always taken for cases of emergency, where a British consul in foreign countries advances small sums to send home persons who become stranded and in distressed circumstances in foreign countries ; and the British government look to us for repayment.
Maintenance and construction of roads, bridges and other necessary works in connection with the Hot Spring reservation near Banff station, North-west Territories, $14,420.

This is the same vote as last year, and is made up as follows : Salaries, of the superintendent, $1,200 ; caretaker, $740 ; caretaker

of the waterworks. $300 ; caretaker of the museum, $200 : estimate for repairs of road east of the bridge, $1,500 ; repairs to other park roads, $1,000 ; new road, $3,000 ; small house for the caretaker of the herd of buffalos, $500 ; care of buffalos and other animals, including $600 for caretaker, $1,500. Then, it is necessary to put In a pipe for the distribution of the hot water, which is one of the attractions of the park, $500 ; clearing land, $500 ; miscellaneous, $1,500 ; general contingencies ii} superintendent's office, $1,000. We ask for a vote of $2,000 for the puchase of animals. We have now about twenty-six (head of buffalo, and a number of elk. I am satisfied the experiment we have inaugurated of starting a herd of buffalo will be a great success. They are breeding very satisfactorily.
Cost of litigation (Department of the Interior) $1,000.

We have always taken that vote, or ever since I have been in charge of the department, to meet any odd case that might turn up where legal expenses are incurred. Cases arise where small costs have to be incurred in connection with the administration of timber lands. It is altogether a provisional vote. We expended last year $170 on two cases.
To provide for the survey of the boundary between the ..Yukon territory and British Columbia from Teslin lake to Alsek river, $20,000.

This is for the purpose of sending a survey party to survey the boundary line between the Yukon territory and the province of British Columbia. The boundary is the 60th parallel of north latitude, and the operations of the survey party are set forth in some notes made by the Surveyor General.
Is the Mr. White-Fraser on that -survey party the inspector of mounted police who has lately been in South Africa ?
No. Mr. White-Fraser is a surveyor. My deputy tells me that he has a brother in the Mounted Police.

Is this a joint survey on behalf of this government and the province ?
The MINISTER OF THE INTERIOR No.
Is there anv arrangement by which the line established will be binding ?

Not yet. We undertook it at first at the request of the provincial authorities, and as my hon. friend will see, knowing what the parallel is. I presume it would be advisable, as my hon. friend suggested, before Mr. SIFTON.
going on with that work, to have an arrangement with the British Columbia authorities, so that there may be no question about it. I do not anticipate there will be the least difficulty, because we are doing the work practically at their request.
At the same time I think it would be desirable that an arrangement should be made.
I quite agree with the hon. gentleman.
i understand that the work will only cost $12,000 for the present season, and the minister has asked for $20,000. What does he want the other $8,000 for ?
There are two parties : Mr. White-Fraser's party is estimated to cost $8,000, and Mr. St. Cyr's is estimated to cost $12,000.
How was this boundary fixed ? Was it fixed by Imperial statute ?
Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: Originally creating the province ?
When British Columbia came into confederation she came in with her boundaries.
Which were fixed by Imperial Act ?
Yes.
Has the boundary never been ascertained on the ground until now ?
No.
How have you got along in regard to jurisdiction ?
Until the last year or two there was nobody there, and it is only for the purpose of meeting the actual necessities of the case that we are going over it now.

Will the hon. gentleman have some more of those maps sent to me? The people of my county are very much infatuated with them, and they have been writing to me about them.
Some resolutions reported.
The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES (Hon. Sir Louis Davies) moved the adjournment of the House.
What business shall we expect to-morrow ?

A few Bills may be taken up. and we will go on with supply. If the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals is
[DOT]2701

well enough, he will go on with his estimates.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: And if not 7
If not, we will take up some of the Interior estimates.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.
